author: fernandoschiavi
summary: With a touching story, revolutionary technology, "Avatar" also includes, in its narrative, several allegories relevant nowadays
text: Although the main narrative of "Avatar" is a reinterpretation of the basic premise of the legend of Pocahontas and brings the concept of an intruder who finds himself inserted in the middle of a new culture and comes to love it in the best "The Last Samurai" style, it is It's the way Cameron tells his story that really stands out. It's interesting that the filmmaker put so much effort into the background and creating a new world that this steals all the public's attention, and this isn't a bad thing. Jake is unable to feel, with the feet of his human body, the soil of Earth or Pandora, the moment when he takes on the body of his Avatar and experiences the texture of dust again with his fingers is touching. Likewise, we do not see the outside of our planet, with the film only presenting us with this alien environment.Appearing as a kind of sci-fi western, "Avatar" surprises by revealing itself to be a kind of "Dances with Wolves" via "The Matrix" and with ample hints of "The Mission", in an unusual combination that, sprinkled with mysticism (the Na'vi worship a well-known deity like "Eywa"), ends up working very well. Echoing the conquest of the Old West, with its bloody conflicts between colonizers and North American Indians, Cameron's script makes no secret of the fact that it sees the Na'vi as the redskins (here blue skins) who were decimated and expelled from their lands by white men, which is reflected even in the aliens' clothes, their war cries and their predilection for archery. Living in perfect communion with the planet, the natives hunt enough to survive and reverently hand over the souls of their prey to the goddess Eywa - and by falling in love with Pandora and her people, Jake undergoes a transition very similar to that of Kevin Costner in his film 1990, growing his beard and hair and abandoning the military analytical coldness that he had adopted as his mission.For the protagonist's conversion to work, however, Cameron must also illustrate to the viewer what is so special about Pandora - and he does this in an impeccable, almost obsessive way. Creating a new world completely from scratch, the filmmaker spends the first ninety minutes of projection in an absolute immersion in that universe, introducing us to a completely original and fascinating fauna and flora, from the fluorescent plants that glow under Jake's feet or they shrink from a simple touch to the gigantic animals that share space with tiny insects and the Na'vis themselves. The amount of detail is such, in fact, that at no point do we have the slightest doubt that that planet really went through millennia of evolution to reach that point - and that everything we are seeing could actually exist somewhere in the cosmos without the idea sounded absurd.Completely created on a computer, the "locations" seen in Avatar are photographed in an absolutely realistic way, presenting a palpable solidity and reacting incredibly naturally to "light sources" - and when we see sun rays crossing the treetops and reaching the characters or the foliage, we have the impression that Cameron found some way to shoot his project on alien soil, such is the photorealism of what we see (and the colors with which the filmmaker works never cease to enchant, from the fluorescent purple of some plants to the intense orange of the hide of a flying beast). Cameron created an entire geography, fauna and flora for his world, as well as a culture peculiar to the Na'vi. In this sense, we note that the filmmaker's passion for the underwater world persists, as the design of certain elements of the forest is very reminiscent of some creatures from our sea depths, with such similarities being more accentuated in the Tree of Souls and the seeds of the sacred tree. Likewise, the design of the aliens combines an elongated structure and humanoid features and limbs, achieving a harmonious balance that allows, for example, us to see Neytiri as a creature obviously very different from humans, but still strangely sensual. Furthermore, the avatars of Jake and the scientist Grace impress by adapting the characteristic features of Sam Worthington and Sigourney Weaver to the Na'vi appearance, which is as admirable as the care with which the textures of their skin were created, showing pores, protuberances and protuberances always convincing.However, none of this would be of any use if the digital characters didn't move naturally - and what James Cameron achieves here with the help of Peter Jackson's WETA is something that, in comparison, makes Gollum from the "Lord of the Rings" trilogy look a broken puppet. Using the performance capture technique, which uses the actors' performances as the basis for the body and facial expressions of their digital versions, the "Avatar" technical team achieves a result unlike anything we've seen before - and every slight nod of head, restrained smile, gaze aversion and hesitation in gesticulation emerge with the clarity of a real performance, making the experience of seeing those gigantic blue creatures talking in front of us on that gigantic screen always fascinating (and this is a film that should be enjoyed in movie theaters). Furthermore, if one of the biggest problems with digital characters has always resided in the still life of their eyes, Cameron seems to purposefully challenge this enemy by conceiving the Na'vis as beings with immense eyes - and full of life.James Cameron (like Peter Jackson) sees technology as a means of telling stories, which makes all the difference in the world. So, when we see Jake's avatar in action for the first time, what makes us care about the character is not his technical perfection, but the fact that Jake, a paraplegic, can barely contain his joy at being able to move his limbs again. Toes, defying the scientists monitoring him to be able to run again after years of immobility. Likewise, the Na'vi version of Grace may be a fabulous copy of Weaver, but it is the kindness of her smile and the enchantment conveyed by her eyes as she witnesses indigenous culture that endear her to the viewer. In fact, just as Andy Serkis deserved to be honored for his performance in "The Lord of the Rings", actress Zoe Saldana certainly deserves applause for transforming Neytiri into a creature that combines sweetness and hardness, softness and rigidity, in a complex and deeply profound performance. Touching - and the girl's efforts become very clear throughout the screening, as no animator would be able to create all those subtleties of interpretation without the actress's performance in the studio. Meanwhile, Michelle Rodriguez embodies without any problem the type of character she always plays, but with competence, that of the tough woman who is always present in Cameron's works, from Sarah Connor from "The Terminator" to the lady- from the adventurous house from "True Lies", to the brave Lindsey Brigman from "The Abyss" and, of course, the unbeatable Ellen Ripley and the soldier Vasquez from "Aliens, the Rescue".Speaking of the military, the biggest disappointment I had in relation to this film was its main villain, Colonel Quaritch, played by Stephen Lang. Totally one-dimensional and with no apparent motivation other than wanting to kill all the Na'vi. In a year in which we had Colonel Hans Landa in "Inglourious Bast*rds", it is simply too little for a villain to rely solely on a more elaborate look and a masculinity so rich in testosterone that it makes the macho heroes of 1980s action cinema look like the Mary Poppins. The film's other antagonist, executive Parker played by Giovanni Ribisi, is also extremely caricatured, see the scene that introduces him, with a golf club in his hand. Appearing little and even a little erased by Quaritch's "male" presence, it is clear that, despite his disastrous actions, he is not an essentially "evil" man, just a greedy and ignorant human being.But as if the touching story, revolutionary technology and intriguing characters weren't enough, "Avatar" also includes, in its narrative, several allegories that are extremely relevant in the contemporary world, starting with its clearly ecological message - and it is a credit to the filmmaker who let us really start to care about the preservation of that alien ecosystem. However, perhaps even stronger is his anti-war protest and the courage to portray the American military as intolerant and prejudiced war beasts: thus, it is not long before Colonel Quaritch mocks the Na'vi religion and employs the rhetoric of "terror against terror" - and Cameron is not at all subtle when presenting the collapse of an important structure for the aliens as the fall of the World Trade Center, complete with ash rain and everything.With an exciting and action-packed third act (another specialty of the director), "Avatar" has an impeccable pace, using its first half in a deliberately slower way to build the narrative and introduce the characters and their universe and gradually stepping on the accelerator as the screening approaches its end - and even then, Cameron and his two editors don't indulge in the wild cuts that would make everything confusing and inelegant. And, as already mentioned, even though the script has its share of shaky dialogues (a notorious weakness of the director-writer) and a small twist in the third act that sounds dangerously like Deus ex Machina, these mistakes are a small sin compared to the that the film achieves as a whole.James Cameron again draws attention and now his shot is much more perfect than "Titanic" or even the "Terminator" franchise. He literally created a universe so tangible and real that we have the planet Pandora as a place to be visited, not a computer illusion. Apparently, James Cameron's current formula has been working, simple ideas with beautiful packaging. Seeing is believing. "Avatar" is a film to be seen and rewatched in the cinema several times.

author: DGPTA
text: Man...Avatar. What a really, genuinely, sincerely, disappointing release.Literally everything about the movie is amazing..........except the story. Which, unfortunately, is the most important part about a movie.The dialogue, the acting, the world building, the casting...obviously the special effects, which are just incredible...all amazing. This movie did literally everything right.Except the plot. Which is just...awful.It's literally as lazy a plot as you can think of, one that is in no way based in reality. It's like a 6 year old watched Ferngully: The Last Rainforest and wanted to make their own version of it.Like, what is this massive, MASSIVE army installation doing on an alien planet brimming with unique, beautiful life, including a peaceful native species?And when I say massive, I do mean massive. What the **** does a peaceful alien planet need this many machine gun shooting, knife wielding mechs for? Hundreds of missile loaded gun ships? Giant bombs capable of wiping out half a planet?Like...why? Huh? Makes no sense at all.Look I'll be the first to acknowledge how awful humans can be, and the especially awful things they've done to indigenous cultures. But no, I'm sorry, if humanity discovered a planet like Pandora, they would NOT bulldoze its most sacred lands and violently commit bloody genocide on the innocent bow-and-arrow wielding natives. That simply would not happen.As half the base is also scientists, clearly humanity is not at a point where we're all war hungry evil world conquering biological beings bent on galactic destruction. And clearly the people on Earth know about the Na'vi. Governments, committees, checks and balances, those clearly still exist. Even the military installments on our own planet are not this decked out, which is currently full of resources to bulldoze and capitalize on. Why would they have it on an alien planet millions of lightyears away, and not prioritize scientific discovery and establishing relations with a freakin' gorgeous, mystical, peaceful alien race?There is just no way this sort of behavior would be a thing, and it TOTALLY kills all the other things this movie did right. It's just...dumb.Sorry, but no. Humans suck, but in the case of a gorgeous alien world like Pandora, they would not suck to this extent, which makes the plot seem like nothing but a lazy, agenda driven narrative.I cannot emphasize enough I am fully aware of western imperialism and the atrocities committed. Which is exactly WHY this would not happen to this extent in the future. It just wouldn't. They put so much effort into making this a "real" experience, while completely ignoring the one ACTUAL thing that would make it real.The plot should have involved humans working WITH the Na'vi to stop a unstoppable force on their own planet, or even ANOTHER alien race...literally anything but what they did would have been better.Ok, rant over. Just severely disappointed cause this could have been an amazing, world changing experience. But instead they chose to go with...this.It does look amazing though, even 15 years later it's still one of the best looking pieces of cinema out there, far more so than many of the CGI action fests that have come out since.Very unfortunate.

author: The-A-list
text: "Avatar," directed by James Cameron and released in 2009, was nothing short of a cinematic revolution when it debuted. The film was lauded for its groundbreaking visual effects, immersive 3D technology, and breathtaking visuals that brought the lush world of Pandora to life. But beyond its technical feats, "Avatar" has been a subject of both praise and criticism for its storytelling, themes, and characters.At its core, "Avatar" is a retelling of the classic "stranger in a strange land" story. Jake Sully, a paraplegic Marine, arrives on the planet Pandora as part of a military operation that aims to extract valuable minerals from the planet. However, Jake finds himself torn between his human obligations and his newfound connection with the Na'vi, Pandora's native inhabitants. Cameron navigates this moral dilemma with a sweeping narrative that makes heavy use of visual and emotional spectacle.The visual effects in "Avatar" are its most talked-about feature for a reason. Even a decade later, the CGI work remains impressive. From the bioluminescent flora to the intricately designed creatures inhabiting Pandora, the level of detail is astonishing. The 3D technology used was groundbreaking at the time and gave audiences an immersive experience that was both novel and captivating.However, the film isn't without its shortcomings. One of the major criticisms revolves around its storyline, often labeled as derivative. The film's plot has been compared to a range of sources, from "Dances with Wolves" to "Pocahontas," for its white savior narrative and its somewhat formulaic take on cultural assimilation and imperialism. Despite its otherworldly setting, the themes and characters sometimes lack originality, making the storyline predictable for some viewers.Another point of contention is the film's handling of cultural appropriation and the white savior trope. While "Avatar" attempts to tackle issues of colonialism and environmental destruction, some viewers felt that it didn't delve deep enough into these subjects, offering instead a rather superficial critique that left many yearning for more nuanced discussion.Despite these criticisms, "Avatar" did shine in its portrayal of strong female characters. Sigourney Weaver's character, Dr. Grace Augustine, is a compelling and multi-dimensional figure. Neytiri, portrayed by Zoë Saldana, is another strong presence, breaking away from the damsel-in-distress archetype often seen in blockbuster films.The film's sound design and score also deserve mention. Composed by James Horner, the music of "Avatar" successfully elevates emotional beats and complements the visual grandeur. Subtle audio cues in the soundscape make Pandora feel like a living, breathing ecosystem, further enhancing the immersive experience.In conclusion, "Avatar" stands as a monumental achievement in film technology, setting new standards for visual effects and 3D cinema. While its narrative and thematic depth may not be as revolutionary as its visuals, the film provides a captivating look into a fantastical world, and it serves as a pertinent allegory for some of the most pressing issues of our time, such as environmental conservation and cultural respect. Despite its flaws, it remains an essential cinematic experience that continues to inspire discussions over a decade after its release.

The intricate details of the Na'vi, Pandora's indigenous humanoid species, their culture, language, and connection with nature, are brought to life with meticulous care and creativity.The performances are equally captivating. Sam Worthington shines as Jake Sully, a paraplegic marine who gains a new lease on life through his avatar. His journey from reluctant participant to passionate protector is both convincing and engaging. Zoë Saldana's portrayal of Neytiri, a Na'vi princess, is equally compelling, lending depth and passion to her CGI-enhanced character.At its heart, "Avatar" is more than just a visually stunning film. Cameron infuses the narrative with potent themes of environmental consciousness, cultural respect, and the destructive power of greed. While the storyline follows a somewhat familiar path, the film's thematic depth and strong character development ensure that it never feels trite or predictable.The groundbreaking 3D technology used in "Avatar" sets a new standard for the film industry. Cameron's innovative motion-capture techniques, along with top-notch CGI and 3D effects, create an unparalleled level of immersion. The film's action sequences, from high-speed chases through Pandora's floating mountains to the epic final battle, are thrilling and expertly executed.In conclusion, "Avatar" is a cinematic marvel that combines innovative technology with impactful storytelling and compelling performances. Its mesmerizing visuals, compelling narrative, and thematic depth make it a must-see film for any cinema lover. In the world of Pandora, James Cameron has created not just a movie, but an experience - one that will leave you awestruck and eager for more.

summary: Avatar is a triumph in every sense of the word. Its groundbreaking visuals,
text: Avatar, directed by James Cameron, is an epic science fiction film that takes viewers on a breathtaking adventure into the lush and visually stunning world of Pandora. Released in 2009, this groundbreaking movie not only pushed the boundaries of filmmaking technology but also delivered a captivating story that resonated with audiences worldwide.Set in the mid-22nd century, Avatar transports us to a distant planet called Pandora, inhabited by a humanoid species called the Na'vi. The story follows Jake Sully (Sam Worthington), a paralyzed Marine who becomes part of the Avatar Program, which enables humans to control genetically engineered Na'vi bodies. As Jake immerses himself in the Na'vi culture and falls in love with a Na'vi woman named Neytiri (Zoe Saldana), he finds himself torn between the interests of the human corporation and the preservation of Pandora's natural beauty.One of the most remarkable aspects of Avatar is its groundbreaking use of 3D technology, which revolutionized the film industry and set a new standard for visual immersion. James Cameron's masterful direction and attention to detail transport the audience into a vibrant and breathtaking world, filled with stunning landscapes, exotic flora and fauna, and awe-inspiring action sequences. The 3D effects enhance the sense of depth and realism, making the viewing experience truly immersive and unforgettable.Beyond its technical achievements, Avatar's story touches upon important themes such as environmentalism, imperialism, and the destructive nature of human greed. It raises thought-provoking questions about the relationship between humanity and nature, and the consequences of exploiting resources without considering the long-term effects. The film's narrative, while familiar in its structure, is executed with finesse, emotional depth, and powerful performances from the cast.Sam Worthington delivers a compelling performance as Jake Sully, capturing the complexity of his character's transformation and inner conflict. Zoe Saldana shines as Neytiri, portraying a strong and courageous Na'vi warrior with remarkable depth and sensitivity. The supporting cast, including Sigourney Weaver, Stephen Lang, and Michelle Rodriguez, further enhance the film with their excellent performances.In addition to its visual and narrative brilliance, Avatar boasts a mesmerizing musical score by James Horner, which perfectly complements the film's emotional beats and enhances the immersive experience. The score combines haunting melodies and tribal rhythms, adding another layer of richness to the already captivating world of Pandora.While some critics argue that Avatar's plot bears similarities to other films, its execution, technical achievements, and the immersive nature of the world it creates set it apart. James Cameron's vision and meticulous attention to detail make this film an unparalleled cinematic experience.In conclusion, Avatar is a triumph in every sense of the word. Its groundbreaking visuals, compelling story, and strong performances combine to create a mesmerizing journey that transports audiences to a world beyond their wildest imagination. Even years after its release, Avatar remains an enduring masterpiece that deserves to be experienced on the big screen.

author: jamesrupert2014
summary: Relentless social messaging in blue-face - a rewatch
text: Jack Sully (Sam Worthington), a paraplegic Marine is embedded with the threatened natives on Pandora by vivifying a hybrid synthetic body, an 'avatar', and soon begins to sympathise with their existential plight. Thirteen years after seeing it in the theatre, I rewatched James Cameron's sci-fi eco-epic while flying across the Atlantic on a small screen a foot from my nose, a venue that unfortunately undercut the film's strengths (the spectacular special effects) while leaving its weaknesses (the hackneyed characters, the story and the preachifying) even more pronounced. While an outstanding 'action' director, Cameron is not the most subtle of helmsmen, so his blue-skinned indigenous Na'vi are almost cloyingly spiritual and righteous, while the interloping humans, led by greedy, callous suit Parker Selfridge (Giovanni Ribisi, apparently channeling Paul Reiser's 'Carter Burke' from Cameron's outstanding 'Aliens' (1986)) and vicious reactionary war-head Colonel Miles Quaritch (Stephen Lang) are stripped-down ciphers with few redeeming qualities. The complete lack of nuance makes 'Avatar' almost a parody of the 'white saviour' trope (an effect heightened by the blatantly human-inspired spiritual rites of the aliens, who seem to mimic a blend of every oppressed culture on Earth). As the core of the interspecific strife is "unobtainium" a vaguely defined über-Macguffin of near infinite value to humans (and presumably worthless to the Na'vi), the entire story is clearly intended to be taken as one giant metaphorical condemnation of colonialism (a social message that Cameron pounds into the viewers mercilessly). I was both impressed and unimpressed in 2010 and remain so. The film is a milestone in cinematography, design, and image rendering but otherwise is a simplistic, moralizing screed that could have been so much better. The box-office thought otherwise...

author: mmarab91
summary: A Visually Stunning Adventure with a Few Hiccups - Avatar
text: Avatar, the groundbreaking film by James Cameron, presents audiences with a visually stunning world that pushes the boundaries of modern filmmaking. It undoubtedly offers a unique and immersive cinematic experience, but beneath the awe-inspiring visuals, the plot feels forced and lacks smooth transitions between scenes, relying heavily on familiar and stereotypical tropes.First and foremost, the film's visual effects are nothing short of exceptional. The lush and vibrant world of Pandora, brought to life with remarkable attention to detail, is a true visual marvel. The imaginative flora and fauna, combined with breathtaking action sequences, transport viewers to a mesmerizing alien landscape. Cameron's use of cutting-edge technology and 3D cinematography enhances the immersive experience, making Avatar a groundbreaking technical achievement.However, where Avatar falls short is in its plot execution. While the film presents an intriguing premise of humans versus the indigenous Na'vi people and explores themes of environmental destruction and cultural clashes, the narrative feels formulaic and predictable. The characters, particularly the human protagonists, often fit into stereotypical roles and lack depth, making it difficult to form a strong emotional connection with them.Moreover, the transitions between scenes can feel abrupt and disjointed, resulting in a disjointed narrative flow. The pacing suffers as a result, as the film tries to balance the spectacle of action sequences with the need for character development and world-building. It occasionally feels as though certain scenes were included solely for the sake of showcasing the visual effects, rather than serving a clear narrative purpose.Despite these flaws, Avatar's strengths lie in its technical achievements and immersive world-building. The film's environmental message resonates with viewers, highlighting the importance of preserving our natural resources and respecting indigenous cultures. The attention to detail in creating the Na'vi culture and language is commendable, providing a level of depth to the world of Pandora.In summary, Avatar's stunning visual effects and immersive world-building make it a must-see film for its technical achievements alone. However, the forced plot and lack of smooth transitions between scenes detract from its overall impact. While the film manages to deliver an entertaining adventure, it relies on stereotypical character tropes and fails to reach its full potential as a truly groundbreaking narrative. Nevertheless, Avatar remains a visually impressive spectacle that left an indelible mark on the world of cinema.

text: Avatar is a science fiction film directed by James Cameron. The movie tells the story of a paralyzed former Marine named Jake Sully, who is sent to the planet Pandora to participate in a program that aims to extract a valuable mineral. Jake, who is tasked with infiltrating the Na'vi by using an avatar, finds himself caught between the two worlds and must choose a side.The sustainability aspects of the film are evident in its message of environmental conservation and the consequences of exploiting natural resources. The movie emphasizes the importance of respecting the environment and the need to protect it from greed and destruction. Representing this idea through the Na'vi people and culture, the film symbolizes the balance of natural world, and the interdependence of all living beings. Across the globe, people recognize it for its stunning visuals, memorable characters, and engaging plot. I love Avatar's portrayal of the Na'vi culture, and their connection to natural world. By displaying the planet's pain through the Na'vi, I resonated with their desperation and suffering, and how that all life endures pain when greed and monetary value are held in higher regard than everything else.Overall, I believe Avatar is a visually stunning and thought-provoking film that effectively conveys the importance of sustainability and the need to respect the environment. author: vanapalliakshaya
text: Did see Avatar for the first time a while ago, and didn't know what to make of it. To me it felt like a visual feast if little else. Re-watching it again, I found more strengths, but there are several weaknesses that prevent it from being a masterpiece.Starting with Avatar's strengths, it is absolutely mind-blowing visually. The cinematography, landscapes, scenery, colours, make-up and effects are outstanding and are by far and away Avatar's strongest asset. I also liked the score, it is certainly not the best score I have ever heard, but it had some very nice moments, while Cameron's direction is competent, the message admirable, and the finale well and truly explosive. I also loved the flying sequences, they were breathtaking.The acting in general is a mixed bag. Sam Worthington is a charismatic enough lead, while Zoe Saldana is strong and spirited. Stephen Lang is an enjoyable and over-the-top villain of the piece too, however Sigourney Weaver is somewhat so-so, doesn't help really her character isn't that interesting while Michelle Rodriguez and Joel Moore aren't given very much to do.What didn't work so well is that Avatar's story, with themes of love in a time of chaos and man alone in a hostile environment, is rather simplistic and predictable. I also felt it took a while to get going, and that the relationship between Jake and Neytiri was on the dull side. And is it me, or does this film drag at times, particularly towards the end? Now don't get me wrong, I liked the concept, it wasn't exactly original, as I often heard it described as "Dances with Wolves in Space with rip-offs of Pocahontas and FernGully"- but I am not going to join those who say that- I have to admit regardless of its originality or lack of it the concept intrigued me. Then there is the dialogue, which is nothing special and never quite rings true. There are some amusing moments but a vast majority of the dialogue in the middle of the film never quite convinced or came across as cheesy. The characters also came across as rather clichéd, especially Giovanni Ribisi's, and the character development was lacking.So all in all, Avatar does have a lot of strengths, but a lot of weaknesses too. I will say I preferred it over The Hurt Locker, which to be honest left me cold, but I think I would be stretching it a bit if I said it was 5-star masterpiece.

author: ryannoel-84353
text: "Avatar" is a cinematic masterpiece that transports audiences to an otherworldly landscape of incredible beauty and danger. Director James Cameron's vision of Pandora, a lush and vividly realized planet inhabited by a vibrant ecosystem and a humanoid race known as the Na'vi, is truly breathtaking. With groundbreaking technological advancements in motion capture and 3D filmmaking, "Avatar" sets a new standard for immersive cinematic experiences.The film's cast delivers standout performances, with Sam Worthington leading the way as Jake Sully, a disabled former Marine who finds himself caught up in a conflict between the Na'vi and a mining corporation seeking to exploit the planet's valuable resources. Worthington brings a sense of vulnerability and determination to his role, while Zoe Saldana shines as Neytiri, a skilled warrior and member of the Na'vi tribe who becomes Jake's guide and ally. The chemistry between the two leads is palpable, and their relationship serves as the emotional core of the film.The supporting cast is equally impressive, with strong turns from Sigourney Weaver as the head of the Avatar program, Stephen Lang as the ruthless military commander determined to crush the Na'vi resistance, and Giovanni Ribisi as the corporate executive overseeing the mining operation. Each character is well-drawn and brings their own perspective to the conflict, adding depth and complexity to the story.Of course, it's the film's technical achievements that truly set it apart. Cameron's use of motion capture technology allows for incredibly lifelike performances from the actors playing the Na'vi, who are seamlessly integrated into the stunning visual effects that bring Pandora to life. The film's 3D presentation, while perhaps seen as a gimmick by some, adds an immersive depth to the film that truly enhances the viewing experience. And the score by James Horner is a sweeping and emotive work of art that perfectly complements the film's themes and visuals.While "Avatar" is undeniably a groundbreaking film in many ways, it's important to note that its story and themes are not entirely original. The film draws from a range of science-fiction and fantasy tropes, from the colonialist narratives of films like "Dances With Wolves" and "Pocahontas," to the technological and environmental concerns of works like "Blade Runner" and "The Matrix." However, Cameron's skillful execution of these familiar themes and his ability to create a fully-realized and immersive world make "Avatar" a truly memorable and impactful film.At its heart, "Avatar" is a politically charged film that raises important questions about environmentalism, colonialism, and the destructive power of unchecked corporate greed. Its message is both timely and timeless, reminding us of the urgent need to protect and preserve our natural world, while also highlighting the dangers of exploitation and domination.In conclusion, "Avatar" is a visually stunning and emotionally resonant film that showcases the very best of modern filmmaking technology. Its cast, score, and direction are all top-notch, and its themes are both thought-provoking and relevant. While it may not be the most original film in terms of its story and themes, its execution is undeniably groundbreaking and it remains a must-see cinematic experience for anyone who loves science-fiction, adventure, or just great filmmaking.

author: Banchode88
text: I saw AVATAR today. It was a boiling 40 degrees Celsius in Australia. I caught a bus and train to get there. I spent months on a forum before that. Incremental stops included a scriptment, stills, a teaser, a foot, AVATAR day and a full trailer. Now released I have had many reviews to read which have been mostly very positive.It is a marvel to watch. The opening scenes are very sci-fi with a glimpse of low gravity aboard a space-craft. Sam Worthington fills us in with a short narration. He is taking over his diseased brother's role in the AVATAR program. These opening scenes are actually among the most effective 3D in the film, pulling you into this story, tracking shots putting you into the steps of the characters.I jump ahead, like the film, to The world of Pandora which is lush with earthly life as seen through pulp fantasies. The rendering of this world is terrific. The life and activity is in the plants as much as it is the animals. Wonder is generated with this ambitious creation. Cameron has lifted the bar. The CG is the best I have ever seen. Everything you have heard is true. The 3D enhances this with leaves falling and swaying branches life-like in the foreground.The realisation of the Navii is also ambitious. They are CG but there are many moments that make you think they are real and in terms of the story they are more than good enough to propel the narrative with strong emotional content.I went into this film knowing mostly everything within it. Hours of reading, some from the treatment and pages of the recent reviews. It is very much a family film like "Nealz" said in his IMDb review. There is a moment where one of the ferocious animal species that earlier were attacking Jake are seen with a litter, the children in the audience loved the cute pups! The spiritual side of this film is much better than expected. It is in fact a beautiful story. The structure is classical film-making but with amazingly new scope in CGI to express grand images. An epicThe journey that Jake takes through Pandora is lovely. He is taken in by the Navii and explores their culture, language and habitat. Natirii, the female Navii he meets while lost, helps him through this journey. This is a love story of both soul mates and with a wider picture. Existential connections with the natural world. Personal destiny.I had tears in this film. I tried to hold them back but by the roll of credits they came. This is a movie that I have anticipated for so long. I think the ingredients of its story and my connection to this films production gave me a very emotional response. I cant imagine this disappointing any of the fans on the board. Keeping in mind that it is a family film but delivered everything I wanted.Expect a special edition. After AVATAR is a hit, a special edition will make its way to the cinema. I can understand why they would cut the earth scenes and it works. The actual film seems pretty brisk and it could also have more padding out. You want more of it and that is a triumph for this type of film running two and a half hours. It is a good balance because at two and a half hours AVATAR is aimed directly at the cinema going audience. Broadly appealing with elements for everyone. My earlier prediction of a billion or more world-wide seems safe.I don't want to go on about visuals too much but the lovely shots of the natural wonderland of glowing life in still 3D shots is magical. Something to take kids to see. Floating tiny neon life jellyfish their way through the air with grace. The monkey-like extra-limbed creatures with the peeping eyes flock through the forrest quickly. The creature design is done in a clever way with the motion of a living thing. The action is over the top, epic, frenetic and a new take on the battle sequence.James Cameron didn't stuff this up. He probably pressed the studio way beyond their comfort zone with the time, money and effort that has gone into this. Sam Worthington is excellent casting choice. Sigourney Weaver ads frank reason. Stephen Lang chews the scenery as the ultimate you know what. Zoe Saldana is beautiful as Jakes guide into this world and.I went to the cinema and it was a very hot day. By the time I left the cinema, the streets were wet with rain. A warm humidity was thick in the air. Lightning splashed my walk to the train station with white light. I honestly wondered if It was my time to be struck down with a bolt of electricity from the sky.Watch this film. It is destined to become a childhood classic to many little-ones too young to be on this forum. It will be talked about at high school by male and females as spectacular. It will be watched multiple times by fans. I loved it but beyond my appreciation for the film itself, is the the message of love permeating from this movie that I hope enters the zeitgeist like elements of Cameron's other stories have. At its heart is a soul. AVATAR is an achievement in many technical departments but I wouldn't say the story is deficient. It is a beautiful experience and the story is surprisingly what I loved most.

summary: A perfect movie for my 400th review
text: In the wake of the new Avatar finally granting me with its presence after 13 years of waiting I've decided to rewatch this masterpiece of James Cameron's and to be honest - it still holds up very strong.I may have seen it only once or twice, I'm doubtful on that, but I remember it impressed me so much that I was still able to produce some scenes from the memory even after thirteen years - and I forget movies pretty quickly after watching it once or twice - and that says something in favor of Avatar. Sure its story isn't new or unheard of, the narrative is pretty foreseeable but it's the way the story is handled that's the most important part.I caught myself staring in awe at the screen, sometimes not even blinking for long not to miss out a single detail, single movement that James Cameron and company have created for the viewers. To say that the nature of Pandora is astonishing will not do it justice, it's impeccable, remarkable and one of a kind; the frame is filled with colors to the brim and its flora and fauna add up just as many different aspects to this strange beautiful world.Avatar is James Cameron's child, he not only wrote, produced and directed it but also co-edited it and his perfectionism is palpable throughout the movie. Sam Worthington has done an incredible job also, both on screen and as his avatar self and I just can't understand why this talented actor was mostly absent from movies since 2009. The rest of the cast is not less impressive, especially I would like to single out Giovanni Ribisi and his greedy corporate businessman who really stood out among your usual movie villains.Avatar as a cinematic experience is perfect in every sense of it but even the most perfect picture gets shattered if nothing stands behind to support it. And behind it is a simple yet touching story of a brand new world and the same old world, how the strong always pick on the weak, how love, trust, friendship and loyalty can become more to life than life itself, how death can become just another step on the way to immortality, how great things are achieved if only people unite, and many other little things. One can even bring up the environment and protection of the world forests to the table - that's how many sides there are to this movie.Avatar is a great motion picture, it changed the game back in 2009 and I believe time will give it a classic status which it truly deserves.

author: LunaticTide
summary: Great storytelling on a truly epic scale
text: When I saw James Cameron's Avatar for the first time it was simultaneously the first time I'd ever seen a movie in an Imax theater and to say that my mind was blown would be a vast understatement. Storytelling on this grand a scale had only happened a few times in my life by this point (primarily the Star Wars prequels and the LOTR films come to my mind) and to see the lush world sprawling out in front of me damn near made me forget that I thought the theater was going to collapse into ruin from how loud it was.Rewatching it over a decade later I'm so happy to report that the CGI has aged incredibly well. If not for that this film would be a hard rewatch considering 90 percent of it is generated. But hell yes, the visuals still feel real, from the majestic floating rocks to the spectacle of the bioluminescent forest floors of Pandora.James Horner's score is up among his best work here, even if it at times uses some of the same motifs he wrote for Titanic. The acting, the writing, the heart. It's all believable, and when you can do that with an entirely fabricated world you really have to give it up to James Cameron's tireless dedication to original and sincere storytelling. More than a decade later it still pays off.

author: MaryCallend
summary: A film that transports you to another world
text: One of the reasons why "Avatar" has resonated with so many people is its stunning visuals. The attention to detail in creating Pandora is awe-inspiring, from the lush forests to the floating mountains and the diverse flora and fauna. The use of motion capture and 3D technology brings the world to life in a way that was previously unheard of in film, and the film's action sequences are breathtaking to behold.Aside from its technical achievements, "Avatar" also has a strong message about respecting nature and the consequences of our actions on the environment. The film's themes of conservation and respect for different cultures are powerful and still relevant today, more than a decade after its release.While the film has been criticized for its derivative plot and its depiction of the Na'vi as a simplistic, noble savage stereotype, it has also been praised for its immersive world-building and the emotional connection it creates with the audience. "Avatar" is a film that can transport you to another world, and that is a rare and precious thing in cinema.

However, he soon becomes embroiled in a conflict between the human military and the indigenous people, the Na'vi, and must choose where his loyalties lie.I've rated a 7 out of 10 for its impressive visual effects and action-packed storytelling. The film's use of cutting-edge technology to create the vivid and imaginative world of Pandora was groundbreaking at the time, and it still arguably is. It still certainly remains a landmark in the history of cinema and CGI. However, some of the film's themes and characters feel a bit formulaic, and the plot can be pretty predictable at times. Overall though, Avatar is an entertaining and visually stunning film that is worth a watch, especially for fans of sci-fi and special effects.

author: seruanyre
summary: Experience the wonder and awe of 'Avatar'
text: "Avatar" is a cinematic masterpiece that transports audiences to a whole new world. James Cameron's directing and writing is top-notch, creating a visually stunning and emotionally engaging story that will leave you on the edge of your seat. The world-building is incredible, with every detail thoughtfully crafted to immerse viewers in the alien world of Pandora. The performances, especially from Sam Worthington as Jake Sully and Zoe Saldana as Neytiri, are outstanding and add depth to the characters. The use of groundbreaking technology and special effects is seamlessly integrated into the film, making for an unforgettable viewing experience. Overall, "Avatar" is a must-watch for any film lover and a true testament to the power of cinema.

author: vithiet
summary: A must see no matter what.
text: I saw it in the theater back in 2009 when it came out and it can't be overstated how technologically and visually groundbreaking this movie was then, in typical James Cameron fashion. Fourteen years later I am revisiting it (the Extended version) to prepare for the sequel and it hasn't lost much of that grandiose epicness. For that alone I would recommend Avatar to anyone. That said the story itself is not much to rave about unfortunately. It's a tale that has been told countless times, using the same tired tropes and is overall pretty predictable. But what it lacks in originality is balanced by great directing and it's still an amazing ride to go on.

author: hidhircloud
summary: James Cameron's direction is nothing short of masterful
text: The film's plot centers around a paraplegic Marine (Worthington) who is dispatched to Pandora on a unique mission, but becomes torn between following his orders and protecting the world he feels is his home. The film's themes of environmentalism, imperialism, and the ethics of war are expertly woven into the story. The acting is strong across the board, with particularly noteworthy performances from Sam Worthington and Zoe Saldana.James Cameron's direction is nothing short of masterful, creating a sense of wonder and awe throughout the film. The film's score, by James Horner, adds to the film's atmosphere and keeps the audience fully immersed in the world of Pandora. The film's cinematography, production design, and special effects are all groundbreaking, setting a new standard for the industry.The film's pace is brisk and the editing is tight, keeping the story moving forward and preventing it from dragging. The dialog is well-written and adds depth and complexity to the characters and the story.In conclusion, "Avatar" is a true cinematic masterpiece that will leave you in awe. The film's stunning visuals and groundbreaking special effects are matched by its thought-provoking themes and strong performances. James Cameron's direction is masterful, immersing the audience fully in the world of Pandora. The film's themes of environmentalism, imperialism, and the ethics of war make it a thought-provoking and engaging viewing experience. It left me feeling like I was part of the journey and it will definitely stay in my mind for a long time.

author: dalyons-09311
summary: Amazing CGI but Doesn't Rely on It
text: Without a doubt, Avatar's CGI is amazing. The groundbreaking use of motion capture was a huge step forward that changed cinema forever. But I used to think that the story ended there, and that if Avatar came out today, it wouldn't make as much money because it would blend in with everything else and that the CGI wouldn't blow me away as much now. Boy, was I wrong. I first saw Avatar around the time it came out and just saw it a second time when preparing for the sequel. For starters, the CGI still holds up. Despite being made in 2009, it looks better than anything that's come out recently. But more than that, equally as impressive as the artwork and detail is the imagination. It would be one thing to have incredible CGI on Earth, like in The Avengers, but Avatar creates the whole world of Pandora that's nothing like anything we've seen, with islands floating in the air and crazy landscapes. To pull off something that creative with CGI is an incredible feat. Every single frame is beautiful. Normally you'd need an animated movie for something like this, but Avatar's CGI is so good that they can pull it off in live action. So much time and care was put into it. But even then, some people argue that the CGI is all it has going for it and that the story isn't very impressive. I have to disagree there. Sure, the story is simple, but I'm fine with simple as long as the execution is effective, and Avatar is executed to perfection. The pacing is perfect despite the long runtime, and the movie effectively establishes the setting and lore, builds up the drama while creating the emotional connections between the characters, and then escalates to a climax that features a battle on the scale of Endgame. The final battle is visually impressive, emotionally charged, well choreographed, massive, and exciting. Unlike the sequel, if this movie had normal CGI, I would still love it. The fact that it has groundbreaking CGI is simply a bonus. Avatar deserved the reception it got.

author: tnelson2-374-411051
summary: This is how you do a blockbuster.
text: I'm writing this review after watching this film the night before seeing it's extremely belated sequel at the cinema.Honestly, I think this film still looks utterly amazing even if was released today. The scale, the scope, the attention to detail is still simply beyond anything that was ever released before or since.James Cameron is responsible for a chunk of my absolute favourite movies. The Terminator, Aliens, The Abyss, T2, True Lies, Titanic - they are all masterpieces of action/sci fi blockbuster cinema with every release representing a massive leap in the technical side of the craft in one way or another, and it feels like this film is a cumulation of these amazing movies. You can see the 'lived in' military feel of aliens and the first terminator here - he has realised the APC and mech suit from his 1986 masterpiece in their fullest glory, the CGI and lighting from T2, the gorgeous luminosity from the ET's in the Abyss, the thudding action of true lies, the epic sweep of Titanic - it all manifests here and then some.The visuals here though at the end of 2022 are frankly astounding still, from the cold military feel on the human side to the lush, gorgeous, colourful world of Pandora this film is a visual treat from start to finish. The human's technology looks utterly realistic and plausible, with every ship, screen and weapon looking like it actually exists instead of it being fantasy tech. Each animal and plant, wether it's something attacking our heroes or a background creature looks like it's had the utmost of thought paid to it's design, colour and sound. Put simply, it creates a world that you have never seen in your wildest dreams and it all works in harmony with everything in this beautiful movie. 13 years on and to me, it still looks pretty much perfect and still above every other blockbuster ever made.And boy does James Cameron know how to direct an action scene. He was already the master pretty much but here you can see it in all it's glory. Every action scene is crisp, clear, coherent yet visceral. Just witness for example the brief scene where the dog type beast near the beginning of the film gets hold of Jakes rucksack - the camera pans around the scene, in slow mo for a few seconds whilst jake wriggles free and attempts to escape, it's a simple yet effective scene that sums up the directors skill in this field, which basically reads 'unmatched' - it's just a small yet subtle reminder of this amazing director's skillset in crafting intimate action scenes or massive set pieces, of which there are many in this.The biggest criticism that most people level at this tends to be the derivative plot, and if I'm honest, it's still a valid criticism.The thing is though, I simply don't care.This film is so utterly immersive, in ways that nothing has ever been before, it just makes up for any storytelling shortcomings. The world building here is off the scale amazing, you really feel like Pandora is a living, breathing place - it's not unlike one of the recent Rockstar games in that you lose yourself in this amazing environment and it seems almost odd when you have to extract yourself from it at the end and rejoin the real world.Big screen entertainment doesn't really get a higher endorsement than that does it?Yes the story is something you will have seen before, but it is well executed, does exactly what it needs to do and no more. It still manages to hit some excellent emotional beats and to be honest, if it were a complicated plot it would detract from what this movie says and does. It has a strong environmental and anti war message which is central to the narrative here and works just like the themes of motherhood in aliens and fatherhood in T2 etc. It's what I come to expect from James Cameron - simple and effective storytelling.For me, this is just an absolute lesson in blockbuster filmmaking and is a must see. I saw this in 3D IMAX in 2009 and it was pretty much the best cinema experience I think I've ever had, but even watching this at home on blu ray it still looks cutting edge 13 years later.An easy 10 out of 10. Never underestimate James Cameron.

author: joeravioli
text: Avatar's success was thoroughly unprecedented. No one expected the blue alien movie to be the highest-grossing movie of all time. Though it was marketed as an event film, I remember very little fanfare leading up to it.And then the movie came out. People watched it, reactions were mixed, typically around the center of the critical spectrum. Few loved it, few hated it. Most thought it was just okay. General criticisms were that the movie was just Dances in Wolves in space, it was too long, and overly simplistic. Though it went on to massive, unreasonable financial success, it faded fast from people's memories. In a few years, people remembered it not for its narrative, not for its characters, but for how much money it made. Then again, that really might have been the most interesting thing about it.Before watching the sequel, I decided to refresh my memory. I settled in, braced myself, and started up the film's extended edition.And I have to say: it was pretty darn good.When you know exactly where the story is going and have a general idea of when it's going to get there, it's far easier to tolerate what on earlier viewings you might have considered to be wheel-spinning. Cameron spends so much time not advancing the plot, delivering pretty visuals and character moments with middling, redundant character insights, but they're delivered in such a brilliantly crafted box that it hardly matters. Cameron really is a master craftsman, and it's a joy to take in his vision, particularly in an era of blockbuster cinema when vision is no longer a priority.The film does make some mistakes I can't overlook though, particularly in its treatment of its female lead, Neytiri. Saldana puts in an expressive, passionate performance, but is reduced to a standard tsundere trope. She brings Jake into the tribe, teaches him their ways, and falls in love with him in the process, but she is disappointingly single-minded and flat. Her humanity has no texture; she's more symbol than character.However, the main character is solid. I know this is an unpopular opinion. Worthington definitely struggles with the accent and occasionally abandons it entirely. But he plays the character well. Jake Sully is a good guy, easy to root for. His mistakes we chalk up to general jarhead dumbness, not ill-intent. He's bold, but not obnoxious, confrontational, but not cruel, and most importantly, he approaches the Navi and their culture with an open heart and open mind. Any judgment he may feel towards them is washed away once he immerses himself in their way of life.The movie is long, and the plot is familiar. But these aren't necessarily bad things. Familiar stories are comforting. They're cozy. And Avatar's first two acts are just that. Watching them, I felt the wonder I didn't feel when I watched the film as a child. Understanding just how much Cameron cares about the environment, how much he wants to preserve and protect it is vital to the experience. Avatar remains a film where its creator's love for filmmaking and nature shines through, and that's something I can easily appreciate.

author: seniorscratchy
summary: A Visual Marvel but Lacking in Substance
text: Avatar (2009) is a visually stunning film that showcases some of the most impressive CGI work to date. The lush and vibrant world of Pandora is a joy to behold, and the design of the Na'vi and the other creatures that inhabit the planet is truly breathtaking.However, despite its impressive visual style, Avatar suffers from a lack of substance in its story and characters. The plot is fairly predictable and unoriginal, and none of the characters are particularly interesting or complex.Additionally, the film falls into the trap of the savior complex, with the Na'vi needing the help of the human protagonist to fight back against their oppressors. While the film's themes of environmentalism and cultural respect are admirable, they are not explored in a particularly nuanced or deep way.Overall, while Avatar is a feast for the eyes, it falls short in terms of narrative and character development. If you're looking for a film that prioritizes style over substance, then Avatar may be worth checking out. However, if you're looking for a more engaging and well-developed story, you may want to look elsewhere.

text: "Avatar" is not simply a sensational entertainment, although it is that. It's a technical breakthrough. It has a flat-out Green and anti-war message. It is predestined to launch a cult. It contains such visual detailing that it would reward repeating viewings. It invents a new language, Na'vi, as "Lord of the Rings" did, although mercifully I doubt this one can be spoken by humans, even teenage humans. It creates new movie stars. It is an Event, one of those films you feel you must see to keep up with the conversation. The story, set in the year 2154, involves a mission by U. S. Armed Forces to an earth-sized moon in orbit around a massive star. This new world, Pandora, is a rich source of a mineral Earth desperately needs. Pandora represents not even a remote threat to Earth, but we nevertheless send in ex-military mercenaries to attack and conquer them. Gung-ho warriors employ machine guns and pilot armored hover ships on bombing runs. You are free to find this an allegory about contemporary politics. Cameron obviously does. At 163 minutes, the film doesn't feel too long. It contains so much. The human stories. The Na'vi stories, for the Na'vi are also developed as individuals. The complexity of the planet, which harbors a global secret. The ultimate warfare, with Jake joining the resistance against his former comrades. Small graceful details like a floating creature that looks like a cross between a blowing dandelion seed and a drifting jellyfish, and embodies goodness. Or astonishing floating cloud-islands. Cameron promised he'd unveil the next generation of 3-D in "Avatar." I'm a notorious skeptic about this process, a needless distraction from the perfect realism of movies in 2-D. Cameron's iteration is the best I've seen and more importantly, one of the most carefully-employed. The film never uses 3-D simply because it has it, and doesn't promiscuously violate the fourth wall. He also seems quite aware of 3-D's weakness for dimming the picture, and even with a film set largely in interiors and a rain forest, there's sufficient light.

author: PedroPires90
text: I have no memory of having watched Avatar again since the cinematic experience in 3D on its release and I confess that I was a little apprehensive about what I was going to rediscover after so many years and in a smaller format. The truth is that the film continues to be a very gratifying experience, even seen in our small living room.Avatar's set-up is just as rough as I remember it (and probably the biggest reason I've avoided rewatching it so many times). It's cold, it's too tech, it's too much about "cruel men", and too mechanized and with a huge introduction of stereotyped characters. It's when we get to Pandora and, especially, when Jake meets Neytiri that we find the whole soul of the film and where it completely absorbs us. The story of a love between characters from different civilizations, a forbidden love is nothing new. We know exactly where this is going and Avatar doesn't bother to do anything new narratively. Still, all the discovery of that new world, all the evidence of Jake Sully and all the elements of a different, beautiful and magical culture leave you with your mouth open and I do not doubt that it is where - the bulk of the 2nd act, where the plot theoretically it just builds on the confidence gained by Jake - that Avatar is a huge triumph, going hand in hand with the great works of the genre in history.In the final act - which is too long - the war is shown harshly and cruelly. Beautiful on screen, but tiring and repetitive. The film finds itself once again - as it almost always does - when it takes time to breathe and let those characters and their emotions breathe. From a visual point of view, this will never cease to be fantastic. From the narrative point of view, it's a tired story, but all the elements of a new culture allow us to get closer to their pain in the face of overly cartoonish villains. Anyway, and despite the imperfections, this is an experience that remains unique and a good opening to a strange and magical new world.

summary: A Perfectly Fine Movie, That's Less Interesting Than the Reaction To It.
text: Avatar is a baffling film in a lot of ways. It's hard not to watch this movie objectively, without the knowledge that in late 2009-early 2010, it was LITERALLY the biggest cultural phenomenon in the world. Yet, as many before me have pointed out, it doesn't have the cultural impact you'd expect a film like that to have. It's no Star Wars, it's no Harry Potter, or hell, it's no Matrix, a much smaller and more cerebral, yet easily more impactful film. Avatar's greatest legacy was a brief craze for 3D, totally manufactured by the studios, that died midway through the 2010s as people refused to subject themselves to headaches and a worse viewing experience.It's a film that came, it went, and most of us forgot about it until Disney resurrected it by (bizarrely, at the time) dedicating a whole quadrant of their American theme parks to the World of Pandora. That, and the meme of the supposed sequel coming out (that it's ACTUALLY coming out is kind of mind blowing).It's just...hard to wrap your head around. As if God himself intervened on behalf of James Cameron to brainwash tens of millions of people around the world to go see this thing, sometimes over and over again. To be honest, I think this is why so many people hate Avatar as well.But is that hate warranted? Re-watching Avatar, I can see why it lit the world on fire back in the winter of 2009. Visually, Pandora looks absolutely incredible and truly visually stunning. It's one of the most fully realized, gorgeous fictional worlds ever put to screen. There are some shots in this movie that I still remember, even if the story behind them is quite mediocre. There's a sort of gimmicky aspect to it as well though; because whenever the movie leaves Pandora and the Na'vi, it becomes an objectively worse experience.Avatar's human characters are quite lacking. Jake Sully (a name that couldn't be more appropriate for a generic action hero) has as much personality as a cardboard box and while I think he sort of has to be this "blank slate" for the audience to connect with in an unfamiliar world, Sam Worthington doesn't really do much with this guy. Again, Luke Skywalker, Neo, Harry Potter, he is not.Most of the people fall into very crude stereotypes; the anti-military aspect of this movie feels like something a high school senior would come up with. You have a caricature of a greedy businessman as a villain; you have scientists who of course, act as the bulwark against the evil, rapacious humans who surround him. And of course, you have the Na'vi, about as blatant a recreation of the "noble savage" trope as you could possibly see in the 21st century.Perhaps though, this is WHY Avatar was so successful and why few films have since been able to replicate that success. Avatar is a simple story, a very simple story, and something that inherently, we all sort of understand. Yes, humans really are greedy and destructive. Yes, the military is militaristic (who knew) and at a certain point, that's really bad. Yes, scientists are moralizing and sometimes annoying, but hell, shouldn't they be sometimes?Avatar came out at the right time and struck a chord. It was a time when audiences had come to expect grand visuals and it really was the best looking film ever made. It was a movie about climate change when so many people felt openly denying its existence. It was a movie about space marines when, well it seemed like every video game made was about space marines. Just when we were beginning to get sick of remakes, reboots, and sequels...Avatar was a wholly original, if not derivative, movie that captured the imagination of a generation...for a couple of months.Avatar came out at a time when global cinema felt like a real thing; you could release a movie, day and date, everywhere. Unlike today, where the idea of a Hollywood blockbuster "doing numbers" in China or Russia is unfathomable or we're more isolated than ever, with a majority of audiences curating their own catalogs via streaming services. Avatar felt like an event.It's just funny to think to figure out why this all happened...when the movie is less interesting than the reaction to it.

author: ccminkus
text: Personally, I believe that decisions were made to reflect stereotypical Indigenous traits in Na'vi characters and furthermore, the plot of the first movie was almost identical to Disney's ethically confused depiction of the Pocahontas story. The issue that arises as a product of this is the perpetuation of Indigeneity as a primitive and/or fantastical concept. In the social realm, Indigenous people's identities are often reduced to a measure of authenticity, which is to say that Indigeneity is dependent on how closely someone resembles the portrait of the colonized; the nature of the 'portrait' is debated by many different scholars. For example, decorated author Thomas King claims that the pinnacle of social Indigeneity is what he dubs the "Dead Indian." In this context, Dead Indians are understood as an amalgamation of stereotypical Indigenous traits, such as beads, leather, animal bones, and feathered headdresses, amongst other meaningful cultural elements (King 54). Thus, the homogenization of physical characteristics belonging to distinct Indigenous tribes makes this caricature of the Dead Indian an impossible image to live up to. However, one must also be aware that this caricature - this portrait of the colonized, as it were - exists on the grounds of racial categorization, which as scholar Ian Lopez claims, "has its foundations in "the Anglo emphasis on morphological difference as a trope for social and power inequalities" (Lopez 54). Now you may be asking yourself: what does this have to do with James Cameron's Avatar? Well, a lot, actually.According to scholar Bonita Lawrence, the portrait of the colonized is representative of "the discursive violence that is perpetrated when colonized peoples have their identities reduced to measurable physical traits or to a strict code of categorization" (Lawrence 41). In other words, the Dead Indian and similar portraits of the colonized do affect the lived realities of Indigenous people - often in a negative way - because "race and identity overlap and influence each other" (Lopez 8). Of course, one may argue that the Na'vi are fictitious and therefore do not have any effect on real life: if only that were the case. As it stands, humans are extremely egotistical. We will find traces of humanity in almost anything: animals, inanimate objects, non-physical entities, and the list goes on. It is ignorant to claim that humans can produce anything without inherent human-bias; all we know is... well, what we know! Nothing is original, everything is based off of something - this is the nature of metaphor (a complex thing being understood in terms of a less complex thing... like an alien to a human), personification (...like an alien to... you guessed it: a human!), and yes, even 10ft tall, blue, alien, primate-things fall into this. That said, if we were to completely discard this fact - if we were to assume that humans are capable of creating entirely new things out of thin air that are not based on anything - it is irrefutable that Cameron was drawing his inspiration for his Native characters from portraits of the colonized. What I am proposing here is so far from a stretch that I am essentially pointing out the obvious: Avatar is Disney's Pocahontas with a fresh coat of paint, and that paint is blue... for some reason.In summary, the intentional perpetuation of these stereotypes - naïve, primitive, bow-wielding, braid-wearing, tree-hugging Natives - is a matter of racial discrimination, as it is boiling Indigeneity down to the stereotypical traits that White society dictates, which as was aforementioned, affects Indigenous people's lived reality. I am not asking you to boycott this or any other following Avatar movie because that would be playing a losing game. All I hope to invoke in you is a sense of criticality; we are more than capable of enjoying media content while still being aware of the implications of the piece and choosing to not let these messages affect our way of thinking and/or viewing of racial groups.

He arrives on Pandora at the same time as Sully and operates an avatar.Neytiri, the daughter of the leader of the Omaticaya (the Na'vi clan central to the story). author: Jeremy_Urquhart
text: I don't always rewatch an earlier movie in a series just because a sequel's coming out, but I hadn't seen Avatar since it was in theatres back in either late 2009 or early 2010. I also vaguely remember seeing it twice in theatres, but it's been so long I don't know for sure. Regardless, I'm surprised by how well it holds up now, and even if I lost a little by not rewatching it in 3D, it still looks amazing.To address the elephant in the room: lots of people criticise the story of Avatar. Yes, it blatantly uses familiar tropes, there are stock characters, and the premise itself is similar to Dances With Wolves. However, I watched Dances With Wolves between seeing Avatar in theatres and rewatching it tonight, and Avatar does the premise better. Further, it's just a straight up better movie.We're seeing a lot of effects-heavy, high-budget movies being rushed lately, and it's making modern blockbusters look pretty shaky. The result of the rushed productions is that work is spread too thin among too many people who don't have enough time or avenues of communication to craft the best effects they can. As such, Avatar, despite being over a decade old, looks way better than the vast majority of blockbusters released in the 2020s.James Cameron is clearly a filmmaker who knows what he's doing. He might rely on cliches and familiar story beats, but he uses them so well (and those sorts of things are tools that can be used well or poorly, depending on the filmmaker). I don't know what the premise of Avatar 2 is, but I'm excited to see it this December. After all, given that Cameron also directed Aliens and Terminator 2, the guy knows how to make a great sequel.

author: Holt344
summary: James Cameron is behind one of the biggest films of our time, Avatar is a modern classic - My Ultimate Review
text: With Avatar: The Way of Water being right on the corner, I thought it was time to rewatch it's predecessor "Avatar", but not the theatrical cut but the Extended Collector's Edition. I watched the film once in 3D at the cinema, but afterwards only on DVD so the quality was far from the same but I still found it to be superb. But this time, I watched it on blu-ray and the video and sound quality was excellent. Every single detail on the screen was clearer and just mesmerizing to watch and an extraordinary experience. The extended and deleted scenes found was enjoying the watch and made the experience better, more fuller. The film is set in the mid-22nd century when humans are colonizing Pandora, a lush habitable moon of a gas giant in the Alpha Centauri star system, in order to mine the valuable mineral unobtanium. The expansion of the mining colony threatens the continued existence of a local tribe of Na'vi, a humanoid species indigenous to Pandora. James Cameron's Avatar follows Jake Sully, a paraplegic Marine dispatched to the moon Pandora on a unique mission but becomes torn between following his orders and protecting the world he feels is his home.When I watched this and experienced this film when I was younger, I never really thought about the social commentary behind the film. I'm talking about the Vietnam War and Indian Wars, they're a huge inspiration to the film's story and themes. Other themes are the conflict between modern human and nature, and the film's treatment of imperialism, racism, militarism and patriotism, corporate greed, property rights, spirituality and religion. Cameron truly nailed it, making a story about love and war but also of alienation. He executed the themes perfectly. The imagery too along with the direction and cinematography is brilliant to say the least. James Horner's musical score is so powerful, making it clear that music makes such a difference.Avatar is very much a James Cameron and I strongly believe this is one of his best films, it was better this time when I'm older and seeing it with fresh eyes after these 8 years. It's directed, written, produced and co-edited by James Cameron and has a cast of well known actors playing lead roles: Sam Worthington, Zoe Saldana, Stephen Lang, Michelle Rodriguez and Sigourney Weaver. Whilst the supporting cast has Giovanni Ribisi, Wes Studi and Laz Alonso. The acting is actually quite great and the actors who are in the motion capture suits bring some terrific acting performances. My favorites were Sam Worthington, Stephen Lang and Zoe Saldana. Their performances were top notch and I just love Jake Sully (the character Sam is playing) he's flawed and the most well written character in the film, with a great character arc.The film made extensive use of new motion capture filming techniques and was released for traditional viewing, 3D viewing. James Cameron broke new grounds with visual effects and the technology behind it. He also wanted a fictional language made for the Na'vi population, Paul Frommer who are a professor at the USC Marshall School of Business created it and made Cameron's vision come to life. There's a lot of things in different departments that created this modern classic. But the interesting thing is how the development of Avatar began in 1994, when Cameron wrote an 80-page treatment for the film. But the necessary technology was not yet available to achieve his vision of the film, according to James Cameron. Avatar was nominated for nine Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Director. It won for Best Art Direction, Best Cinematography and Best Visual Effects. Avatar is also the second-highest-grossing movie of all time after Gone with the Wind with a total of more than $3 billion, it also became the first film to gross more than $2 billion. It's one fascinating milestone, the film hit many milestones.I'll end my review with a quote from one of my favorite film critics. Roger Ebert of the Chicago Sun-Times called the film "extraordinary" and gave it four stars out of four. "Watching Avatar, I felt sort of the same as when I saw Star Wars in 1977," he said, adding that like Star Wars and The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, the film "employs a new generation of special effects" and it "is not simply a sensational entertainment, although it is that. It's a technical breakthrough. It has a flat-out Green and anti-war message". I couldn't have agreed more with this. James Cameron's Avatar is a extraordinary film from start to finish, a true modern classic and an epic.
