author: thebackofmyhouse
summary: Not the game changer that is hyped up to be
text: Avatar is the first movie I've watched in 3D. The hype is that it is made to be watched in 3D, and the 3D is not some afterthought tacked onto the movie like some other 3D movies. But being this is my first 3D experience, I'm unable compare Avatar's 3D to other movie's 3D, but from what I've seen, it gives a different experience, but not really essential. I have to admit that 3D does add something to the experience of watching the movie, but what it adds just isn't enough for it to be something that will change how people go watch a movie altogether.Apart from adding something, 3D also takes something away. If you're not used to wearing glasses, then wearing those 3D glasses while watching the movie isn't really "comfortable". You never really forget that you're wearing glasses. The feel of it on your face, and the glass itself gives you a feeling like you're watching a movie through a window. And wearing glasses also makes the movie darker than normal. Some dark scenes become just too dark to see what's happening.But the CG in Avatar really does push the boundaries of what has been done before. What they've really nailed is the facial expressions on virtual characters. That, they got it almost perfect. But as for the human/humanoid body movement, they've got most of it right, but some if it just isn't that good. But one GC element that they made "their's" bio-luminescence. Nobody has done it, and if they have it was never as good as what is seen here. The CG of mechanical things like vehicles isn't the best of what we've seen. Transformers 2 did a way better job of it than Avatar. And the vehicle and mech designs in the movie seems as if James Cameron is stuck in the 90s. They seem dated.In the end, what makes a movie isn't the CG, it's the story. And the story in Avatar isn't a very original story. It is about humans trying to exploit the riches of a foreign planet at the expense of the aliens living there. Sure James Cameron did a great job of fleshing out the environment of Pandora, the alien planet, but as to what takes place on the planet, he could've done better. The dialog is very simplistic, but it's not as Star Wars prequel bad. There's nothing "edgy" to the story. It's very straight forward ,feels like it's a story made for a kids movie. There isn't any plot twists that turn things upside down.So it has beautiful CG, but has a mediocre story. It still can be enjoyable if it has great action. But I'm sad to say that the action does not redeem the movie to enter the "enjoyably fun" category. The final battle is a big one, but I never really got into it. Maybe it's the 3D glasses, maybe it's just the direction, but it didn't work for me. What makes an action scene work is choreography and damage. As for the choreography, there isn't really much opportunity to implement cool choreography in the action scenes as most of the action is organism vs. machine. It's organism vs. orgasm is where choreography can shine. And as for damage, in their effort to keep the movie PG, there is very minimal blood splatter, and the vehicular damage wasn't very dramatic.So there it is. Avatar. A movie that wanted to change things, and change may very well come if enough studios jump on the bandwagon, but if seen as what it is, a movie, it's just mediocre.

author: Troy_Campbell
summary: James Cameron: thanks for the chance to witness a turning point in cinematic history.
text: How often do you get to see a turning point in cinematic history? Not in hindsight, but as it is actually happening? Not often. Those watching The Jazz Singer in 1927 (debut of audible dialogue) or Becky Sharp in 1935 (introduction of Technicolor) experienced it. I wasn't born for another eight years, but I have read and heard that when Star Wars first came out in 1977 people were feeling a similar way; that they were witnessing something never before seen that would change movies from that point on. Has it really been 32 years between motion pictures that have had this impact? Well, revolutionary movies wouldn't be revolutionary if they came along all the time.James Cameron's long-awaited, much-touted 3D motion-capture technique is a step towards the future. What we see on screen during Avatar is nearly impossible to explain with words. But I'll try. Do you think 3D is just a gimmick? Think again. The depth and clarity afforded by the third dimension is invaluable; it immerses you into the action so well that you aren't sitting in a cinema for three hours, you enter a whole new world. Forget the blurry patches to the sides of the screen or the impossibility of seeing things that are moving too fast, as experienced in previous 3D flicks, with Avatar you see everything as if it were real.The digital surroundings that Cameron has created (so he could shoot his actors with mo-cap in an environment that already existed) are awe-inspiring. Pandora is a beautiful forest and jungle-like land, whilst its non-Na'vi inhabitants are exotic and exhilarating in equal parts. The realism of this fantasy world is extraordinary; from the opening shot to the closing credits, Pandora and all its creatures do exist. In addition, and most importantly, the motion-capture technique used for the Na'vi is astounding. Cameron's groundbreaking technology enables the Na'vi to look, move and interact realistically; the smallest of nuances from the actors, including pupil movement, have been mimicked flawlessly onto their digital counterparts.The aforementioned visual revelations are unsurprisingly marvellous during the action sequences – the climactic battle is undoubtedly the standout – however they lend themselves to the subtler scenes just as well. Cameron refuses to use his pioneering invention just for spectacle; he wants it to assist in capturing the minds and hearts of his audience. Take for example a couple of the scenes where the Na'vi fly on their local birdlife. To experience something so graceful and elegant, yet so thrilling and jaw-dropping, is where the real pleasure lies.Most gratifying is not all the optical splendour on offer mind you, it is the powerful tale that it is in aid of. Cameron's account of love, war and nature is more affecting than you might expect. Avatar boasts a screenplay which at times will make you laugh, at times make you cheer and at times make your heart heavy. It never neglects the story and even infuses the action with a surprisingly high level of emotion. A pivotal scene midway through where the humans launch their first attack is genuinely gut-wrenching and shattering; evoking similar feelings you get when watching the atrocities committed in wars gone by. Cameron is greatly assisted by James Horner's booming score too; it's African-esquire sounds giving it an exotic and poignant feel that match the proceedings perfectly.Hollywood's new kid on the block, Aussie actor Sam Worthington, delivers a star-making performance as the conflicted Jake that, along with his turns in Terminator Salvation and the upcoming Clash of the Titans, will surely see him catapult to the top of the A-list. The unrecognisable Zoe Saldana is breathtaking as Neytiri; Sigourney Weaver adds her usual class and elegance as the 'mother' of the Avatar program, Dr Augustine; Michelle Rodriguez gives a career-best performance as the cocky yet likable pilot Trudy Chacon; whilst Stephen Lang makes one heck of a badass.James Cameron: thanks for giving this 24 y.o. his first chance to witness a turning point in cinematic history. It will not be forgotten.5 out of 5 (1 - Rubbish, 2 - Ordinary, 3 - Good, 4 - Excellent, 5 - Classic)

author: rettercritical
text: AVATAR has a soul I saw AVATAR today. It was a boiling 40 degrees Celsius in Australia. I caught a bus and train to get there. I spent months on a forum before that. Incremental stops included a scriptment, stills, a teaser, a foot, AVATAR day and a full trailer. Now released I have had many reviews to read which have been mostly very positive. It is a marvel to watch. The opening scenes are very sci-fi with a glimpse of low gravity aboard a space-craft. Sam Worthington fills us in with a short narration. He is taking over his diseased brother's role in the AVATAR program. These opening scenes are actually among the most effective 3D in the film, pulling you into this story, tracking shots putting you into the steps of the characters. I jump ahead, like the film, to The world of Pandora which is lush with earthly life as seen through pulp fantasies. The rendering of this world is terrific. The life and activity is in the plants as much as it is the animals. Wonder is generated with this ambitious creation. Cameron has lifted the bar. The CG is the best I have ever seen. Everything you have heard is true. The 3D enhances this with leaves falling and swaying branches life-like in the foreground. The realisation of the Navii is also ambitious. They are CG but there are many moments that make you think they are real and in terms of the story they are more than good enough to propel the narrative with strong emotional content. I went into this film knowing mostly everything within it. Hours of reading, some from the treatment and pages of the recent reviews. It is very much a family film like "Nealz" said in his IMDb review. There is a moment where one of the ferocious animal species that earlier were attacking Jake are seen with a litter, the children in the audience loved the cute pups! The spiritual side of this film is much better than expected. It is in fact a beautiful story. The structure is classical film-making but with amazingly new scope in CGI to express grand images. An epic The journey that Jake takes through Pandora is lovely. He is taken in by the Navii and explores their culture, language and habitat. Natirii, the female Navii he meets while lost, helps him through this journey. This is a love story of both soul mates and with a wider picture. Existential connections with the natural world. Personal destiny. I had tears in this film. I tried to hold them back but by the roll of credits they came. This is a movie that I have anticipated for so long. I think the ingredients of its story and my connection to this films production gave me a very emotional response. I cant imagine this disappointing any of the fans on the board. Keeping in mind that it is a family film but delivered everything I wanted. Expect a special edition. After AVATAR is a hit, a special edition will make its way to the cinema. I can understand why they would cut the earth scenes and it works. The actual film seems pretty brisk and it could also have more padding out. You want more of it and that is a triumph for this type of film running two and a half hours. It is a good balance because at two and a half hours AVATAR is aimed directly at the cinema going audience. Broadly appealing with elements for everyone. My earlier prediction of a billion or more world-wide seems safe. I don't want to go on about visuals too much but the lovely shots of the natural wonderland of glowing life in still 3D shots is magical. Something to take kids to see. Floating tiny neon life jellyfish their way through the air with grace. The monkey-like extra-limbed creatures with the peeping eyes flock through the forrest quickly. The creature design is done in a clever way with the motion of a living thing. The action is over the top, epic, frenetic and a new take on the battle sequence. James Cameron didn't stuff this up. He probably pressed the studio way beyond their comfort zone with the time, money and effort that has gone into this. Sam Worthington is excellent casting choice. Sigourney Weaver ads frank reason. Stephen Lang chews the scenery as the ultimate you know what. Zoe Saldana is beautiful as Jakes guide into this world and. I went to the cinema and it was a very hot day. By the time I left the cinema, the streets were wet with rain. A warm humidity was thick in the air. Lightning splashed my walk to the train station with white light. I honestly wondered if It was my time to be struck down with a bolt of electricity from the sky. Watch this film. It is destined to become a childhood classic to many little-ones too young to be on this forum. It will be talked about at high school by male and females as spectacular. It will be watched multiple times by fans. I loved it but beyond my appreciation for the film itself, is the the message of love permeating from this movie that I hope enters the zeitgeist like elements of Cameron's other stories have. At its heart is a soul. AVATAR is an achievement in many technical departments but I wouldn't say the story is deficient. It is a beautiful experience and the story is surprisingly what I loved most. Believe the hype.

author: ed_metal_head
text: James Cameron has been quoted as saying that Avatar will "change the way we watch movies forever". He's right. Avatar is easily the greatest visual feast that has ever graced the screen. This was my first 3D film and I must admit that I thought 3D was no more than a cheap gimmick that movie studios were pushing to get butts into seats. I was wrong. 3D, in this form, is here to stay. It may not be perfect yet, but the first talkies and colour movies weren't either. What's especially impressive is *how* the 3D is used. Most 3D films throw a couple objects at the screen hoping to woo the crowd. Sure, there's some of that in Avatar, but for the most part Cameron uses the 3D to immerse us in his world. There's some impressive stuff outside that too. Picture a room full of people. Why would anyone use 3D for that? Incredibly it works. The depth perception here isn't used for cheap effects but to demonstrate the distance between the person at the front of the room and the person at the back. Subtitles in 3D? Surprisingly, more legible than 2D subtitles.Unfortunately, the movie falls short of perfection. Weeks ago South Park called the film "Dances with Smurfs". A more apt comparison for the plot cannot be found. The movie borrows liberally from Dances with Wolves. Even the diary plot device plays out the same way as it did in Dances with Wolves. It's also disappointing that the trailer manages to reveal the entire plot. I had hoped for a few surprises, but unless you count the theological aspects none were really forthcoming.At this time it should be mentioned that those looking for a James Cameron balls-to-the-wall style action movie will be sorely disappointed. Sure, it ends with a spectacular battle, but there's precious little conflict before. For the most part, the first two hours are all about introducing us to the world of Pandora and its people, flora and fauna. Personally, I was quite happy that some action was eschewed to develop the world, but those with little patience are forewarned.With Avatar, James Cameron has crafted another fine film. It could never have lived up to the massive hype, but it does come close. The technological breakthroughs made for this film will serve cinema well in the coming years. Avatar represents an evolution of cinema. It's just not the revolution it was made up to be.

author: Robert_90
text: Well, here it is.James Cameron's project has been hyped to within an inch of its proverbial life over the years, what with the epic budget, alleged re-inventing of special effects and some admittedly underwhelming trailers full of conspicuously computer-generated blue elves. The question that's burning in everybody's mind leading up to its release this week is: Is it really that great? The answer: pretty much, yeah. But more on that in a bit.For those of you who haven't heard the story, the plot revolves around paraplegic marine Sully (Sam Worthington), who's offered a second chance at life on the lush alien planet of Pandora. The humans on the planet are engaged in a war with the native population, blue humanoid warriors known as the Na'vi, over extremely valuable natural resources. To this end, a handful of scientists (led by a delightfully taciturn Sigourney Weaver) have created an "avatar" project where people control cloned Na'vi in order to get close to the tribes and work something out. Through a cruel twist of fate, Sully ends up controlling one such avatar and from there the story well and truly begins.Now, where do I start with Avatar? The film's a lot of things, but it's obviously not perfect, and I'm not sure whether to address its flaws or good points first. Something tells me I'll go with the flaws first. It's hard to judge them too objectively - it all depends on just how tolerant you can be. I'd probably say the film's worst flaw also plays a huge part in defining just how good (or bad) the film is. I refer of course to the film's copious use of CGI characters. This is a problem that I think will depend on the viewer. Either you're going to find it horribly distracting the whole way through or get used to it after about five minutes. I reckon this is something that is up to every viewer to decide. Myself - I fall into the latter camp. Just as well, because that could very well be the major deciding point in how to judge the film, if only because Avatar is saturated with CGI. Not like that's a bad thing, as a lot of the CGI looks very flash. Avatar's look is pretty damned impressive, all things considered. Between the lush locations, slick gadgetry and veritable cornucopia of action available, I can hardly see how the film's abundance of CGI is a problem. It definitely aims high and hits its mark a lot.With that main issue out of the way, the rest of the film manages to be considerably strong a lot of the time. Once the story gets going, it stays riveting for much of its lengthy runtime. It's well-written, even if one of the central metaphors seems a little too obvious (powerful corporation attacking harmless natives over valuable resources - not exactly subtle) and it managed to keep reasonably surprising all the way to the end. The acting was by and large good; Worthington doesn't exactly shine as the hero, but he performs reasonably well. The highlight is probably Weaver, although there's something to be said for Stephen Lang's battle-scarred colonel, who makes up for a general lack of character dimension with relative ease.The real question remains as to just how great Avatar is. It's definitely an amazing epic in spite of its few flaws and relative lack of originality, so it's admittedly far from perfect. It remains by and large a visual extravaganza if nothing else, and should deserve consideration for one of the better blockbusters of the year (if not necessarily one of the best films). Depending on your expectations, it either wasn't quite as great as it could have been or it was far superior. If you had mixed expectations like I did, it's probably a mix of both. Avatar remains a technically great piece, a bit lightweight in parts, but overall pretty damned good. I'll definitely be checking this out in 3-D, anyway.

author: aiga
text: Today I saw the beginning of a new era – I had the opportunity to be one of the first to see Avatar. I tell you! It is amazing!!! It is a must-see movie. The story just moves fluidly forward and takes you on a magical ride. I must make a remark regarding the much-discussed technological achievements. CGI is incredible! author: NonSequiturL
text: A film with the scope of James Cameron's Avatar was always going to be a risk both artistically and financially, especially in today's economic climate. Whether it will pay off monetarily is a question only time can answer, but this viewer can at the very least attest to it being an artistic triumph.Avatar brings us as close as cinema ever has to actually visiting an alien world. The beautiful environs, the exotic creatures and incredibly lifelike natives of Pandora arrest the senses, visually, aurally and emotionally. The world in Avatar is the true star of the show. The amount of detail and work that has gone into bringing this new world alive is seriously impressive, and it will be a while before we see anything that overtakes it in scope and quality. WETA Workshop and ILM have truly outdone themselves.Relative newcomer, Aussie Sam Worthington provides a solid human heart amongst all the science-fiction/fantasy beauty and Zoe Saldana gives an impressive performance as the 8 foot tall Na'vi, Neytiri. Even though the characters they both play are blue, giant, catlike aliens, they managed to evoke a chemistry and likability that pierces through the special effects.That's not to say that everything is perfect. The story is basic and dare I say, clichéd and predictable. We have seen it plenty of times in all forms of media. The bad guys are cartoonishly evil, and sadly paper thin. The love story, while charming, is also clichéd despite being between man and alien. But in the face of these shortcomings, Avatar is a success because its storytelling lies in the brilliant visuals.Avatar is a beautiful piece of film and a true event. It does exactly what cinema was always intended to - it takes us away from our problems and worries for a few hours and gives us memorable images which will undoubtedly and deservedly enter into the cultural lexicon to stay for the foreseeable future.9.5/10

author: ClaytonDavis
summary: One of the best cinematic experiences ever...
text: Forgive me, I'm going to jump from professional to fan boy for a while here. I haven't had the jitters after a film the way I've had for Avatar in quite sometime. James Cameron's Avatar is the most entertaining and enthralling cinematic experiences of my life. It is incredible, simply put. What Cameron has done here is the most passionate film project put out since Steven Spielberg released Schindler's List. His attention to detail and his zeal for pushing the envelope is so admirable to any filmmaker or actor who will ever do another film from this point on.Avatar is the story of Jake Sully, a paraplegic marine, who replaces his brother on a secret mission to infiltrate the Na' vi, the colony of beings that sit on the planet of Pandora, where there is a precious ore, that sells at a ridiculous amount. When Jake learns the ways of the Na' vi, his feelings and learnings will put him and the people he trusts in dangerous jeopardy.The performances here, in the sense of reacting, becoming, and understanding what Cameron has written are astounding. Not to be confused with a sensational bravura performance from some of the centuries best such as Marion Brando, Tom Hanks, or Diane Keaton; these actors along with the director inhabit these visual transformations with special effects as if they are have lived these beings all their lives. This is all based on character movements and reactions. Sam Worthington, as Jake Sully, is an actor who's on his way to becoming a star. Though he has problems with his Aussie accent often enough in the film, he gets the job done. Zoe Saldana, who plays Neytiri, a Na' vi huntress, is thrilling and electrifying. Stephen Lang, as the rock hard Colonel Miles, takes on a villainous turn to a new level in science fiction. He offers actual emotion and emotes evil to the audience and gains our hatred easily. Sigourney Weaver as the beautiful Dr. Grace, is sufficient enough to have on screen again teamed with Cameron. She lives inside her role with effortless ease, but suffers from some of the typical James Cameron cheesy lines.Narratively the film works perfectly on the cinematic level. The first forty minutes or so require patience and hope as it is the weakest part of the film and offers some dreariness, but when the second act takes off, it's sky high with no limits for James Cameron. Avatar delivers the best action sequences put on film of all time. That is the boldest statement I have ever made in all my years of criticism. I sat on this for two days before charging it out, but I mean it. It is the best visual experience of my life, period.Other than those visuals, the film pops with all the other technical aspects thrown into one. Art Direction is killer as the two worlds blend in perfectly for an acceptable time. The Film Editing is the crowning achievement of the film as it also offers the perfect blend of the two worlds, enticing the viewer and shifting us around. Mauro Fiore is the threat for a Cinematography Oscar this year. It was if the viewer sat down in a chair, put on glasses, and was literally placed on Pandora, spaceships, and floating mountains. The viewer can feel so engulfed by the imagery, you feel like you can smell the leaves from the trees. Avatar is utterly hypnotizing. James Horner's score is some of the best work done in his career. It offers a variable of devastation that moves the viewer to near tears. It goes back to his work on Titanic, where the musical instruments lifted the material immensely. The entire sound team is also locked and loaded for Oscar recognition as the feeling of animals, machines, and arrows buzzing by your head leave you imprisoned in Cameron's exquisite film.James Cameron has come back home ladies and gentlemen Cameron is back, bigger, badder, and mature in his crowning work of his career. Terminator 2: Judgment Day and Titanic do not even compare anymore. This is the film that can blend the fans of those two films together and lock Cameron into your heart. He's a definite spoiler for a directing bid for the Academy Awards. You have admire the raw, natural talent the man has. How could you ever conceive such an experience and put that much effort and work into it and have it pay off? The box office success will surely keep him in the minds of voters for various critics' awards. His screenplay, leaps and bounds better than 1997's Best Picture Winner, is primed, developed and ripe for the taking. Though, you do acquire the tacky and atypical dialogue you expect from a science fiction director of this caliber, you can appreciate the effort and the honesty of it all. James Cameron is everything Michael Bay wishes he was, to put it bluntly.Avatar will bring also great actors putting their best foot forward such as Giovanni Ribisi, who is as underrated as they come. Michelle Rodriguez who exudes sexy like any woman starring in a sci-fi epic. Joel Moore, showing his range outside of his comedic work in Dodgeball: An Underdog Story. And the classy veteran actors, CCH Pounder and Wes Studi, who just simply don't work enough.Avatar is one of the best films of the year. The most exciting, thrilling, and superb work you'll feast your eyes on in any theater this century. Cinema, forever, will remember the benchmark that James Cameron placed not only for himself, but for any man, daring to change the game, the way Cameron did. Avatar is a movie experience to be remembered, and please experience in a movie theater first.***½/****

author: loufalce
summary: A Time Waster that Ain't Worth Your Time
text: An 85 minute movie expanded to 2 and a half hours. James "Titanic" Cameron's less than titanic effort has a paralyzed marine being sent to the Planet Pandora to fetch a substance that can be used as an energy source on a fuel hungry Earth in the future. The CGI effects are OK-but they wear their welcome out fast. The trite and very hackneyed story seems to have been lifted from Dances With Wolves,Pocohontas, Alien, Cameron's own Aliens,The Lost World, Atlantis-The Lost Empire , Journey to the Center of the Earth,and the Wizard Of Oz-especially for the first 20 or so minutes that are filmed in standard format before the film goes CGI,kind of like the black and white opening of Oz before Dorothy arrives there and it goes to color. The planet Pandora itself features flying dragons and blue indigenous natives that are a poor parody of American Indians. It seems as if Cameron is saying that only the white race of people can be the saviors of this world, and that even though the indigenous peoples are very smart, they just don't have the intelligence to fend or themselves.All the clichés are there, the love interest, the greedy industrialist, the strong , liberated woman, etc, etc. For a short time it is eye popping, even dazzling, but from then on it slowly sinks{get it?} into its own pretensions.Worse still, there really is no sense of humor or comedy relief to lighten things up a bit. Its as if Cameron is saying "wow, just look at it. It's awesome, isn't it?". Well, the real fact of the matter is that it is not. Cameron has always been a props and FX director and still has a lot to learn about the human element and character development . Since this ass-buster runs for what seems to be an eternity, why didn't he attempt to make the characters interesting? He knows that today's multiplex bred filmgoers just don't seem to care so he takes the easy way out and gives us an FX movie that is just overkill.It is all style, no substance and leaves you with a cold and empty feeling. I'm sure this movie will probably do good in the awards department, but that does not justify you giving up two and a half hours of your life to see it.You've seen it all before-and much better too.Even the current Planet 51-a not too good sci-fi parody -comedy of an astronaut landing on a planet where the aliens are based on 1950s American pop culture offers some fun and laughs manages to outshine this. This film is just so ordinary that it is a crime.See it if you like-just don't expect too much. Cameron thinks that the CGI effects of this film will be "the next big thing in film-making" Guess again James.If you can wait 9 or so weeks, you'll be able to rent this at Blockbuster.WARNING! Do NOT take little children to see this movie. They will become just as bored as you-only faster.My rating-one star.

author: TheMovieSearch
summary: Its weaker film in the franchise
text: James Cameron's Avatar: The Way of Water is a visually overwhelming return to Pandora, one that proves Cameron is still operating on a scale few filmmakers can even attempt. From the opening moments, it's clear this sequel exists to push cinematic technology forward yet again. The water effects alone are astonishing, creating an underwater world that feels tangible, fluid, and alive in a way modern blockbusters rarely achieve. Every ripple, creature, and reflection feels carefully engineered, making the film a technical marvel first and foremost.At the heart of The Way of Water is a stronger emotional focus than the original film. This time, the story leans heavily into family, legacy, and survival. Jake Sully is no longer just a soldier-turned-outsider; he's a father trying to protect his children at all costs. Neytiri, portrayed powerfully by Zoe Saldaña, brings raw emotion and ferocity, grounding the film whenever it risks drifting too far into spectacle. Their family dynamic adds genuine stakes, especially as their children navigate identity, belonging, and responsibility.The introduction of the Metkayina clan expands Pandora in a meaningful way. Their ocean-based culture, customs, and relationship with the sea are beautifully realized and thoughtfully distinct from the forest Na'vi. These sequences slow the film down, sometimes to a fault, but they also deepen the world-building and reinforce the film's themes of coexistence and respect for nature.That said, the film's biggest weakness is its runtime and pacing. At over three hours, The Way of Water often lingers too long on dialogue and exposition. While the action sequences are breathtaking and expertly staged, they're separated by stretches of repetitive conversations that dilute the urgency. The villain's return feels serviceable rather than inspired, functioning more as a narrative device than a compelling character.Despite these flaws, Avatar: The Way of Water succeeds as an epic cinematic experience. It's a film meant to be seen on the biggest screen possible, not just watched but absorbed. While it may not be endlessly rewatchable due to its length, its ambition, emotional core, and technical brilliance ensure it stands as one of the most impressive theatrical achievements of the modern era and a strong foundation for future installments.

author: TalahaseesLittleBrother
summary: A Visual Spectacle Marred by Familiar Flaws
text: James Cameron's Avatar: The Way of Water (2022) marks a return to the lush world of Pandora, over a decade after the original film's groundbreaking debut. As a sequel, it expands on the epic scope of its predecessor, diving deeper-quite literally-into the oceanic realms of this alien planet. While the film undoubtedly pushes the boundaries of cinematic technology, it stumbles in its narrative execution, recycling tropes that feel increasingly out of step with modern sensibilities. This review examines the film's dazzling technical prowess alongside its more troubling shortcomings.From a technical standpoint, The Way of Water is nothing short of a masterpiece. Cameron and his team at Weta Digital have once again redefined visual effects, creating a seamless blend of motion-capture performances and photorealistic CGI that immerses viewers in Pandora's vibrant ecosystems. The underwater sequences are particularly breathtaking, with fluid simulations that capture the grace of marine life in exquisite detail-from bioluminescent creatures gliding through coral reefs to the intricate play of light refracting through water. The high-frame-rate (HFR) filming technique, employed in select scenes, enhances the clarity and realism of action set pieces, making battles and chases feel palpably intense. Innovations in performance capture allow actors like Sam Worthington and Zoe Saldaña to deliver nuanced expressions through their Na'vi avatars, bridging the uncanny valley in ways that feel revolutionary. Sound design and score, courtesy of Simon Franglen, complement this visual feast, with immersive audio that envelops the audience in the symphony of Pandora's natural world. In an era where blockbusters often rely on spectacle alone, Cameron's film reminds us of technology's potential to elevate storytelling-or at least, to dazzle us into submission.However, these achievements are undermined by persistent issues in Cameron's screenplay, which often feels like a retread of well-worn paths. At its core, The Way of Water echoes the original Avatar's narrative beats, essentially reprising "Pocahontas in space" with a watery twist: a colonial force threatens indigenous harmony, and a human outsider integrates into the native culture to become its savior. This formulaic structure lacks freshness, leaning heavily on predictable plot twists and character arcs that prioritize spectacle over substance. The dialogue, while serviceable, is clunky and expository, with lines that border on the melodramatic-think earnest proclamations about family and unity that fail to resonate on a deeper emotional level.More concerning is the film's tone-deaf handling of indigenous tropes. The Na'vi, modeled after various real-world native cultures, are portrayed through a lens of exoticism that romanticizes their "primitive" harmony with nature while pitting them against technologically advanced invaders. This "noble savage" archetype, complete with spiritual rituals and tribal warfare, feels reductive and insensitive in 2022, especially given ongoing global conversations about cultural representation and colonialism. Cameron's intent may be to celebrate environmentalism and cultural resilience, but the execution risks perpetuating stereotypes rather than challenging them.Visually, while the film's palette is undeniably vibrant, it veers into over-saturation at times. The too-bright colors-neon blues, glowing greens, and fiery oranges-can overwhelm the senses, particularly in IMAX or 3D formats. What aims for awe-inspiring beauty occasionally tips into garishness, detracting from subtler moments and contributing to visual fatigue over the film's lengthy three-hour runtime.In conclusion, Avatar: The Way of Water is a technical tour de force that cements James Cameron's legacy as a visionary filmmaker. Its innovations in VFX and world-building are worth the price of admission alone, offering a cinematic experience that's hard to match. Yet, the narrative repetition, problematic tropes, and stylistic excesses prevent it from transcending its blockbuster roots. For fans of spectacle, it's a must-see; for those seeking depth, it may leave you longing for more substantial waves.

author: filmdixry
summary: Recycled plot within a National Geographic documentary
text: I'll start with the negatives... The bulk of the plot is both figuratively & literally recycled from the first film, so much so that they punctuate said copy & paste plot moments with the same backing track from the original movie. There's a jumble of off-hand plot devices used as the reason for the humans returning to Pandora, but there's at least two that I noticed which somewhat contradict each other. A handful of times Weaver's teenage character gets hints at her own subplot that could set her apart, but it never comes to fruition and the movie leaves every question about her unanswered and unsatisfying. In fact, the choice to have Weaver play this younger incarnation frequently distracts. It's less to do with the idea of an adult playing a child via mo-cap and more the fact that... well, it's Sigourney Weaver. Pitching her voice up and shrinking her Na'vi body down isn't quite enough to bridge the uncanny valley of hearing an icon.My thinking is that Cameron's betting that you'll be too bowled over by what a decade of technological advancement has done for realizing Pandora on screen to worry too much about the plot/characters, and the results speak for themselves.Make no mistake: huge chunks of this movie are absolutely gorgeous. Just about all of the water and underwater effects are rendered immaculately, and there is some genuinely incredible animation at work to capture little micro expressions in the acting which make the Na'vi characters look and feel very real. Stunning visuals are mostly owed to a series of long, scenery-chewing montages that carry very little weight in terms of the story or the plot. The movie is at its best when it's pretending to be the prettiest screensaver you've ever seen in your life. The main character is Pandora itself. The film isn't necessarily about the story, it's about transporting you to another world. The movie should be viewed as itself, not for its purpose of storytelling. The purpose is to be present, to be in that world, to be enjoying and sustaining that feeling.Way of Water really gives the impression that what Cameron is actually interested in with Pandora is the sort of thing you'd find in a National Geographic documentary rather than a blockbuster movie. There's infinitely more care and detail placed into moments of exposition about things like the ins-and-outs of a whaling operation on Pandora than any plot-critical character moment. The creature and tech designs show clear thought and care - even the differences between the forest Na'vi and the reef Na'vi are meticulously crafted and believable. It's just a shame that there's no real story to tell with them, and no real reason to feel invested in them beyond superficial beauty.

author: darkflickx
summary: Stunning Visuals and Intense Action, But a Familiar Story
text: Avatar: The Way of Water delivers an extraordinary visual experience, especially in its underwater sequences, but it does not reach the emotional or narrative impact of the first film. The technical achievement is undeniable. The water environments, creature designs, and motion capture work are some of the best ever put on screen. Every frame looks polished, and the action scenes are executed with remarkable clarity and scale. The film truly shines when it focuses on the Metkayina tribe, their culture, and the unique fighting style that blends water movement with traditional weapons. The scenes involving the bow and arrow combat from flying creatures are among the most thrilling moments in the movie. In a positive sense, the film expands the Avatar universe in a visually rich and immersive way. The world-building feels deeper, the environments are more detailed, and the new tribes add fresh cultural layers to Pandora. The family dynamics bring warmth to the story, and the film consistently emphasizes themes of unity, resilience, and connection with nature. Even though the story follows familiar patterns, the emotional moments still land well, and the film succeeds in creating a sense of wonder. The dedication to technical innovation and world expansion shows how much passion went into making this sequel. However, the story feels predictable and familiar. Many plot points follow a pattern that has been seen before, and the emotional depth that made the first Avatar so memorable is not as strong here. The narrative leans heavily on themes of family, revenge, and survival, but it does not explore them in a fresh or surprising way. While the characters are likable, their arcs do not carry the same weight as they did in the original film. Despite these shortcomings, the movie remains entertaining due to its action, world-building, and visual spectacle. It is a film that excels technically but falls short in storytelling. Avatar Part 1 still stands as the stronger and more impactful film, with a sense of originality and emotional resonance that Part 2 cannot fully match. Avatar: The Way of Water is a visually breathtaking experience with impressive action, but its story lacks the strength and originality of the first film. It is enjoyable, but it does not surpass the legendary impact of the original Avatar.

text:
Movie Review: Avatar: The Way of Water (2022)
Avatar: The Way of Water (2022), directed by James Cameron, is the long-awaited sequel to the original Avatar film. Set more than a decade after the first movie, the story continues to follow Jake Sully and Neytiri as they build a family and fight to protect Pandora from renewed human threats.The most striking aspect of this film is its breathtaking underwater visuals. Cameron pushes cinematic technology even further, creating realistic ocean environments and new aquatic creatures that make the world of Pandora feel richer and more expansive. The detailed animation and motion capture, especially during the underwater scenes, provide a deeply immersive viewing experience.In terms of storytelling, The Way of Water places a stronger emphasis on family, survival, and belonging. Unlike the first film, which focused heavily on discovery and cultural conflict, this sequel highlights parental responsibility and the bonds between parents and children. While the plot unfolds at a slower pace, the emotional moments and character development make the story meaningful.The performances remain strong, particularly Zoe Saldaña as Neytiri, whose emotional range adds depth to the film. New characters from the Metkayina clan introduce fresh perspectives and expand the cultural diversity of Pandora. However, the film's long runtime may feel overwhelming for some viewers.Overall, Avatar: The Way of Water is a visually spectacular sequel that successfully expands the world of Pandora while delivering a heartfelt story about family and protection. Though slower than its predecessor, it proves to be a worthy continuation of the Avatar saga.

author: DerickK-4
summary: Another Technical Achievement For Cameron, But Not As Fresh As The Original.
text: Three years ago after 13 years in the making, James Cameron finally made a sequel to his most popular movie "Avatar". The first time I watched it, I wasn't sure if it would be able to recapture the magic that made the original film the "Star Wars" of its time. Thankfully, the film managed to be another technical achievement that pushed the limits of digital and motion capture filmmaking.Set more than a decade after the first film, the story follows Jake Sully and Neytiri, now raising a family on Pandora. Their peaceful life is shattered when the Sky People return, bringing with them a resurrected Na'vi avatar version of Colonel Quaritch, whose mission is personal and relentless.To protect their children, Jake and Neytiri seek refuge with the Metkayina, an ocean dwelling Na'vi clan whose culture, physiology, and spiritual practices revolve around the sea. As the Sullys learn to adapt to this new environment, tensions rise, old threats resurface, and the family must confront what it truly means to belong, and what they're willing to sacrifice.Great movie sequels are movies like "The Empire Strikes Back" and "T2". These movies expanded on their predecessors and arguably were better films than the originals. Cameron, when he made "T2" understood that he needed to up the stakes and take the story in a different direction that made it one of the most iconic action films of the '90s. Now if "Avatar" was all about discovering Pandora for the first time, then "The Way of Water" is about feeling it. Cameron takes the world of the first movie and expands on it with the introduction of the Metkayina clan and their bond with the intelligent whale like Tulkun. This helps make the world feel more organic and mythic. Much of this happens in the middle of the film where Cameron's passion for the ocean really shines. And since it's been 13 years since the original, the story now focuses on Jake's kids, particularly Kiri and Loak, which gives the film a strong emotional anchor.The biggest selling point of this movie is the extensive special effects that utilize underwater motion capture. The result is breathtaking imagery, fluid movement, and alien marine creatures that look and feel alive. Pandora's oceans are as richly imagined as the forests of the first film. As for the action sequences, they're some of the best that I've seen in a modern film combined with the extensive visual effects. The final act of the film is literally a symphony of tension, choreography, and visual clarityThat being said, the film isn't perfect. The film reuses the same narrative beats from the original film, even recreating some moments from the original, only this time using Quaritch. The film runs too long at over 3 hours and while the underwater sequences are beautifully shot, they bog down the runtime with overly indulgent details instead of using that time to develop its characters. And with such a long runtime, some of the characters wern't developed as much as others due to the heavy focus on VFX.In the end, "Avatar: The Way of Water" is all about immersion into the oceans of Pandora. It's technical innovation, and worldbuilding ambition make it a rare cinematic experience. Cameron isn't just telling a atory. He's inviting viewers to spend 3 hours on an alien world. This is just an instance where VFX come across as overly indulgent and the novelty factor isn't as strong as it was in 2009.

author: AruzhanT-08
summary: The Way of Water Is the Way of Loss and Love
text: Avatar: The Way of Water doesn't try to reinvent the world of Pandora - instead, it slows down and lets us live in it. The film shifts its focus from war to family, from conquest to survival, and that change makes the story feel more intimate and emotionally grounded.At its core, this is a film about parents and children. Jake and Neytiri are no longer just warriors; they are trying to protect their family while adapting to a completely new way of life. The Metkayina people and their bond with the ocean bring a sense of calm and balance, showing another side of the Na'vi culture - one built on patience, connection, and respect rather than constant conflict.Visually, The Way of Water is breathtaking. The underwater world feels alive and immersive, but it's not just there to impress. The ocean becomes part of the story, reflecting both beauty and danger, freedom and fear. The quieter moments - learning to breathe, to swim, to listen - carry as much weight as the action scenes.What makes this film special is its emotional honesty. It lingers on grief, on displacement, and on the painful process of change. The Way of Water is less about fighting enemies and more about learning who you are when everything familiar is taken away - and finding strength in family when the world keeps pushing you under.

text:
Avatar: The Way of Water (2022) is the sequel to Avatar (2009) that was written and directed by James Cameron and it follows Jake Sully living with his newfound family formed on the extrasolar moon Pandora, but when a familiar threat returns to finish what was previously started, Jake must work with Neytiri and the army of the Na'vi race to protect their home. This is a movie that I've been waiting a long time for since it would be the first directorial effort by James Cameron since the first Avatar movie back in 2009 and I got the chance to watch this movie in theaters back in 2022 and it was just as phenomenal as the first movie.Positives for Avatar: The Way of Water (2022):

Regardless of what you think about James Cameron, this man knows how to get the attention of movie audiences with his movies and it's no surprise why they make so much money. This is a movie where you can tell James Cameron put in a lot of resources during the making of this movie and it paid off for him. The cast is still great in their respective roles with Sam Worthington as Jake Sully, Zoe Saldana, as Neytiri, Stephen Lang as Colonel Miles Quaritch, Sigourney Weaver as Kiri, Cliff Curtis as Tonowari, Kate Winslet as Ronal, Jamie Flatters as Neteyam, Britain Dalton as Lo'ak, Trinity Bliss as Tuktirey, Jack Champion as Spider, Bailey Bass as Reya and Filip Geljo as Aonung. There is a lot of attention to detail with every shot of this movie that you can put them on a frame in your house. You still get the themes on the exploration of life and how precious it is with every living creature on Pandora and I felt something for them when they form bonds with each other and when they are horribly murdered by the Sky People. The movie is paced very well with its 3-hour runtime and there wasn't a point where I was bored with what I was watching. The action is directed expertly well especially during the third act which is always the case when it comes to James Cameron's movies. And finally, the movie ends on a note that perfectly sets up the various arcs for our cast of characters in Fire and Ash (2025).Mixed for Avatar: The Way of Water (2022):
The story and characters are pretty simple just like in the first movie and you have seen them done in other movies before with story beats that are very predictable with every character.Overall, Avatar: The Way of Water (2022) was a phenomenal return to the director's chair for James Cameron as well as being a phenomenal viewing experience in the theater for me and I am so ready for Avatar: Fire and Ash (2025) later this month.

author: DavidL-111
summary: A dazzling dive back into Pandora.
text: Avatar: The Way of Water is a visually stunning, emotionally resonant return to Pandora. It's one that reaffirms James Cameron's unmatched talent for immersive world-building. While it doesn't revolutionize storytelling, it absolutely pushes the boundaries of cinematic spectacle.The film's strongest achievement is its breathtaking visual craft. The underwater environments are mesmerizing, bioluminescent ecosystems, fluid motion capture, and a level of detail that makes Pandora feel truly alive. Cameron's insistence on technological innovation pays off; the water itself becomes a character, creating a sense of awe few blockbusters can match.Narratively, the film improves on the original by grounding its emotional stakes in family dynamics. Jake and Neytiri's evolution into parents adds depth to the story, and several of the new characters, especially their children, bring a fresh perspective. Still, the plot sometimes treads familiar ground, and at 3+ hours, the pacing sags in places.Performance-wise, the cast gives convincing life to their digital counterparts. The return of the villain is handled better than expected, adding nuance and moral ambiguity to what could have been a simple retread.Ultimately, The Way of Water is not a perfect film, but it is a remarkable one. It delivers an unparalleled audiovisual experience, a heartfelt story, and a compelling expansion of the Pandora mythos. For anyone who values cinematic ambition, it's well worth diving into.

author: chriss17eu
summary: It seemed impossible to surpass its predecessor after its tremendous impact.
text: The first thing that stands out in 'Avatar: The Way of Water' is its impeccable visual display. James Cameron once again demonstrates his undeniable mastery in the use of light and color. The application of both is exquisite: every frame seems meticulously designed to highlight the beauty of Pandora. It's a visual spectacle that is as appealing as it is carefully crafted, with an art direction that reaffirms the technical perfectionism characteristic of the filmmaker.In this sequel, the visual approach seeks to continue - or even surpass - the achievement of its predecessor. However, there is a certain irony in its execution: despite the hyperrealism achieved, the 3D models paradoxically feel more artificial than in the first film. The animation technology is impressive, especially thanks to the use of the simulcam, but that extreme digital precision can generate a slight sense of falseness at times. Nevertheless, the technical quality is undeniable, and the animation, overall, borders on outstanding.Narratively, the film follows a parallel path to the first installment. Its structure and development inevitably recall the original, though it incorporates the necessary elements to distinguish itself. The inclusion of Jake Sully's children constitutes the main emotional and narrative driving force of this sequel. This decision reconfigures the roles: the protagonist of the first film now takes on a more paternal position, giving part of the spotlight to his offspring, who bring freshness and dynamism to the story. The new characters display charisma, strength, and a convincing chemistry that strengthens the family core of the plot.The aquatic element is, without a doubt, the great innovation. Far from being a mere change of scenery, water becomes an essential component of the narrative and the visual identity of the film. Although it might initially seem repetitive or excessive, Cameron, along with Rick Jaffa and Amanda Silver, manages to incorporate it with subtlety and coherence. The transition between the jungle and marine environments maintains the essence of Pandora while naturally expanding its universe.The story, while not revolutionary, maintains constant interest. It is even more entertaining than the previous one, despite its extended runtime. It's true that some sequences could have been condensed, but the balance between pacing, emotion, and spectacle is skillfully preserved. The length - over three hours - can feel a bit excessive at first, but as the plot progresses, the viewer becomes immersed in the atmosphere and loses track of time. The music accompanies so precisely that it's barely perceived consciously, yet its presence is essential in reinforcing the emotional tone.Overall, 'Avatar: The Way of Water' is a technically exquisite and narratively satisfying work. It's not the best movie in the world, nor does it try to be, but it represents a natural and coherent evolution within the 'Avatar' universe. Its greatest achievement lies in its focus on the Sully family, especially the children, who bring renewed energy. For me, this sequel not only lives up to the original but surpasses it in several aspects, solidifying Cameron as a visual storyteller who continues to push the boundaries of contemporary cinema.

author: sunyx-26086
summary: "Water Remembers" - Review of Avatar: The Way of Water (2022)
text: I love the sequel but the movie is way too long, so i have to speed up 1.5x to save time ! Why do they have to make sequel so long ! And i have to watch avatar 3 in cinema for three hours again!Ames Cameron has never been shy about making sequels that are bigger, wetter, and more obsessive than anyone expects, and Avatar: The Way of Water is exactly that kind of movie. Thirteen years after the original film turned blue aliens and 3D into a global event, he returns to Pandora not to reinvent the plot but to grow the world outward and downward, into the oceans, families, and spiritual ecology of this planet. It is, in many ways, a simpler story wrapped in a staggering technical showcase: a chase movie about a father trying to keep his children safe, told through some of the most convincing underwater performance capture ever put on screen.We pick up with Jake Sully (Sam Worthington), now fully Na'vi and chief of the Omatikaya clan, living with Neytiri (Zoe Saldana) and their growing family. They have two biological sons, Neteyam and Lo'ak, a young daughter Tuk, and they have adopted Kiri, born from the avatar of Dr. Grace Augustine, and Spider, a human boy left behind on Pandora. For a while life is good. But humans return to Pandora with a harder mandate: not just mining, but full scale colonization. Among them is a Recombinant version of Colonel Quaritch (Stephen Lang), resurrected in Na'vi form with his memories intact and a personal vendetta against Jake. Realizing his very presence puts the forest clan in danger, Jake makes the painful choice to move his family across the planet to seek shelter with the Metkayina, an oceanic clan led by Tonowari and Ronal. The rest of the film alternates between the Sully family learning the "way of water" and Quaritch relentlessly closing in. When he finds them, the conflict pulls the coastal people into a war they did not ask for.The main characters this time are less about Jake alone and more about the kids. Jake is still a solid center-older, more cautious, occasionally overbearing. Neytiri remains fierce and emotionally raw, especially when her children are threatened. But it is Lo'ak (Britain Dalton) and Kiri (Sigourney Weaver, playing a teenager with uncanny ease) who carry the emotional weight. Lo'ak is the second son who keeps failing to meet his father's standards; his reckless bravery and his bond with a banished tulkun (the film's jaw dropping whale like beings) gives the story its heart. Kiri, who feels a mystical connection to Eywa and to Pandora itself, adds a spiritual mystery and reminds us that the avatar-human hybrid experiments have consequences far beyond one movie. Even Spider, constantly torn between his human heritage and his Na'vi family, gives the Quaritch plotline texture. Quaritch, for his part, is a more interesting villain in recom form-still brutal, but now forced to experience the world through the very body he used to hunt.The themes are clear. First, it is about family as a communal, not just biological, organism. Jake keeps saying, "Sullys stick together," and the movie tests that mantra over and over. Every child makes mistakes, and every mistake puts someone else in danger, but they keep choosing each other. Second, it is about displacement and the pain of asking for sanctuary. The forest Na'vi are visibly out of place among sea people who breathe, move, and even think in rhythms shaped by water. Cameron lets us sit in that awkwardness, making assimilation a real process instead of a montage. Third, it is about kinship with nature. The Metkayina do not just hunt the tulkun; they have deep emotional bonds with them. When hunters arrive to slaughter them for a single extract, it is not just an ecological crime, it is a personal one. That gives the third act its moral fire. Finally, it is still about colonial violence. The human military is more mechanized than ever, burning coasts and killing sentient whales to fund Earth's survival, and Cameron is not subtle about who the invaders are.Cinematography and visual design are where the film becomes something special. Shot in high frame rate segments and built on underwater performance capture that took years to perfect, the ocean sequences are mesmerizing. Cameron and cinematographer Russell Carpenter fill the frame with shafts of light, swirling sand, bioluminescent coral, and quick turns of Na'vi bodies that actually move like they are buoyant. The camera often drifts with the characters, mimicking the way water suspends everything, so even quiet scenes-Lo'ak bonding with his tulkun friend, Kiri lying in a sea of glowing anemone like plants-feel transportive. Above water, the film continues the sweeping aerial views of the original, but the color palette is cooler, all aquas and teals instead of the forest's deep greens. The Metkayina village, grown along massive mangrove structures, looks like something that could actually exist on Pandora. Even the human tech is more tactile this time: crab shaped submersibles, hulking sea going gunships, smaller, nastier mech suits that are designed for faster, closer fights.As an action director, Cameron remains unmatched in clarity. The final hour is basically one extended siege and rescue, but it is staged in layers-ship, decks, below deck, sinking hull-so we always know where everyone is. He crosscuts cleanly between parents, children, villains, and even animal allies so that the emotional stakes stay locked in. When tragedy hits, it lands because we have spent real time with these kids in training, fighting, bickering, and playing. The water, so beautiful earlier, becomes a trap, and Cameron leans into survival thriller beats he loves (you can feel echoes of The Abyss and Titanic in the flooded corridors).On the strengths side, the most obvious is the world building. Pandora's seas are so richly imagined that it feels like we could spend another entire film just exploring them. The second strength is emotional focus. For all the tech and spectacle, this is ultimately about a dad trying not to lose his family and about kids trying to earn respect. That is simple, but simple works. Third is the sheer technical bravado. Even viewers who are lukewarm on the story tend to admit they have never seen water and digital characters integrated this convincingly. Fourth, the film expands the Na'vi culture without contradicting what came before-different physiology, different tattoos, different tools-and that makes the planet feel alive.There are weaknesses. At over three hours, the movie is long, and viewers who are not naturally enchanted by Pandora may feel the middle stretch-where the Sully kids keep getting into local trouble-drag. Some of the dialogue, especially Jake's stern dad lines, is blunt. The villain side is better than in the first film but still not particularly nuanced; Quaritch's hinted inner conflict is more set up for future installments than payoff here. And because the film is so focused on this one family, the broader stakes of humans colonizing Pandora recede a bit into the background. We know Earth is dying and the RDA intends to make Pandora home, but here it mostly translates into "the bad guys are hunting the Sullys."Even so, Avatar: The Way of Water succeeds at the core thing it needs to do: make you care about returning to this world. It trades the first film's "wow, aliens" feeling for "wow, this place has depth," and that is a smart evolution. It gives us new clans to love, creatures to grieve, kids to root for, and a villain whose relationship to our heroes is complicated enough to fuel sequels.Conclusion: The Way of Water is a reminder that sometimes the biggest movies earn their bigness. It is overlong in spots and occasionally on the nose, but it is also heartfelt, visually jaw dropping, and committed to telling a story about family and belonging inside a science fiction epic. If Cameron's plan is to keep diving deeper into Pandora, this is a strong second plunge.

author: danielgroza
text: In the digital age of AI, CGI, cinematic universes and Marvel throwing special effects around like it's free candy, James Cameron's sequel to his cult-classic "Avatar" reminds us that there's one more giant they didn't account for. Not to the degree of the first movie in 2009, but "Avatar: The Way of Water" still looks and sounds like something from the future. Even today, its special effects and visual creativity remain a reference point for this billion-dollar industry.The movie is just short over three hours, and not soon enough I could see why. There are prolonged moments of visual delights in which the very blue Na'vi navigate their native world of Pandora in all its glory. It could feel like gloating but watching any of the Avatar movies and complaining they spend too much time showing off it's missing the point. Cameron crafted this world with love, how could he possibly not flaunt it? He was always fond of visual storytelling, preferring to use smoke and mirrors to advance his plot. So, naturally, this becomes tricky when the plot involves a very human--or Na'vi?--story of family and unity in times of turmoil.The story continues where the first one left off with Jake Sully (Sam Worthington), now living a full Na'vi lifestyle with his significant other Neytiri (Zoe Saldaña). Now, having four kids, Jake's priorities have switched to full on fatherhood. "A father protects, that is his purpose"--he says, as his kids call him sir. He holds up a very conservative household yet one which is built out of necessity rather than principle. His children are survivors, their life will not be easy and he knows that. And not soon enough, as an old enemy resurfaces, he now must choose whether he will flee or stay and fight. His paternal struggle is the most human element in Cameron's movie, yet one which is always foreshadowed by the inevitable bombardment of flamboyant visual set-pieces which, granted, are made as good as they could possibly be, and more than welcome. But more often than not, I couldn't help but think about Jake's inner struggle and how I would love to dig deeper into it.But, fine, nevermind that. Cameron has other points to make; stuff related to what put him on the map: ambitious set-pieces, hypnotizing visuals and larger than life action scenes, yet all of them story-driven which is what makes him great--or, at least, better than most of his kind. So, yes, the king of visual storytelling hasn't returned after 13 years because he never left. But like any great craft master, he needs time to perfect his masterpiece. It's not dry yet, but it's getting there.

text: "Avatar: The Way of Water" is a dazzling return to Pandora that fully capitalizes on its aquatic environments. author: MrBoMzIMDb
summary: A Stunning Return to Pandora with Mixed Depths
text: Avatar: The Way of Water, directed by James Cameron, marks the long-awaited sequel to the groundbreaking 2009 original. The film revisits Pandora, immersing audiences in its lush environments and aquatic ecosystems with breathtaking visual effects and state-of-the-art motion capture technology. While the world-building is undeniably spectacular, the narrative balances between action spectacle and emotional resonance, sometimes struggling to maintain cohesion under its visual grandeur.The story follows Jake Sully (Sam Worthington) and Neytiri (Zoe Saldaña) as they navigate familial responsibilities and intertribal conflicts, introducing a new generation of Na'vi, particularly their children, whose development adds fresh dimensions to the saga. The performances are solid, with Worthington and Saldaña providing grounded emotional cores amid epic set pieces. The film also explores themes of environmental stewardship, legacy, and survival, though some plotlines feel formulaic and predictable, echoing familiar beats from the original film.Cinematographically, the sequel is a triumph; the underwater sequences are immersive and fluid, pushing the boundaries of visual storytelling. Composer Simon Franglen's score complements the grandeur and emotional beats effectively. However, the film's extended runtime and occasional narrative indulgences can challenge pacing, leading to moments where spectacle overshadows character development.Avatar: The Way of Water succeeds as a cinematic spectacle and a continuation of Pandora's story, though its narrative and thematic depth do not fully match the originality of its predecessor. Fans of the original will be enthralled, but casual viewers may find it less emotionally compelling despite its visual mastery.Rating: 7/10 - A visually breathtaking sequel with strong emotional moments, yet hampered by predictability and pacing issues.

author: I_Ailurophile
summary: Doubts, faults, and scrutiny can't dampen the splendor of an overall terrific cinematic spectacle
text: I'm a rather cynical, skeptical person by nature. Broad appreciation of the 2009 film was paired with subsequent wry observation and commentary that has taken on a life of its own in the years since. Learning that James Cameron intended several more sequels raised an eyebrow. Sights unseen, learning that this first sequel of 2022 was nominated for major awards inspired utmost disbelief. All the best technical ingenuity and innovation in the world - what Cameron is known for, such as with 'Terminator 2,' and 'Titanic' - doesn't count for much if the writing and direction don't hold up. I recall enjoying the predecessor but saw it once in theaters and not since; could 'The way of water' really be as strong and deserving as it's made out to be?Such reservations go first and foremost for the computer-generated imagery that constitutes the overwhelming majority of the sights to greet us, all but a relative sliver. I'm someone who will always, always prefer practical effects and tangible creations to post-production fiddling, for with rare exception digital wizardry ages rapidly, and looks worse the more we see of it; only when employed with the greatest of care and hard work will such visuals hold up, no matter how outdated they may be. Gratifyingly, in this case, they mostly do. This feature is nothing if not a wonderland for the eyes, and with even more diverse landscapes than what we saw before, the world of Pandora is unspeakably beautiful. Forests, skies, islands, and the ocean both above and below water are all mesmerizing - and to my pleasure, this splendor extends to fauna and flora, to the production design and art direction including structures, crafts, and props, and even to some character designs, like Kiri, or the distinctions between races of Na'vi. Pandora and its inhabitants are as beautiful as they are fierce, not to mention wonderfully imaginative, and by this measure alone the action-adventure is a terrific success. It's still true that I'd quite prefer a wider away of physical goods, yet with visions this magnificent, I can easily abide.Thankfully, the excellence of 'The way of water' doesn't end there. Tremendous thought and care went into the sound effects, realized with luscious audio design, and extending even to the Na'vi language, and the languages of endemic wildlife. Russell Carpenter's cinematography is as smart and dynamic as it is sharp and vivid. I adore Simon Franglen's original score, a panoply of rich, varied themes that very ably complement the proceedings at all turns. Cloaked as they may be behind motion-capture technology and digital falsehood, I'd be remiss not to also commend the cast for fantastic performances. In this case I don't even mean established foremost stars, like Sam Worthington, Zoe Saldaña, Stephen Lang, or Kate Winslet (generally all very good, mind you), but more to fresher faces portraying the younger Na'vi, such as Britain Dalton (Lo'ak), Trinity Bliss (Tuk), Bailey Bass (Reya), Filip Geljo (Aonung), and in a better, meatier role than she had last time, Sigourney Weaver. Pair all these high quality facets with the most lovingly penned instances of scene writing, and real world-building, and at its best the picture absolutely inspires awe and wonder - and elsewhere, as intended, thrills, disgust, and other more raw emotions. At its best, this picture really did earn its high praise.I did say "at its best," however. For as good as 'The way of water' mostly is, part of me still questions if it was necessary in the first place, and it bears definite flaws and shortcomings. Some dialogue is very good; some is achingly awful, and both apply to instances of voiceover narration. Some character writing and direction elicits tired sighs, primarily where antagonist figures are involved, and frankly I find myself doubting all the writing surrounding the character Spider. In some sequences intended to inspire awe the doing is blunt and gawky; some scene writing is downright messy. I also think that even over the course of more than three hours, the narrative tries to do too much. Action-adventure, earnest exploration of the world of Pandora, and direct commentary on our reality by way of this fictional one are all worth delving into; solid and cohesive as the plot is, it nevertheless overextends itself in some measure. Above all, speaking of that direct commentary: this movie is so dubiously heavy-handed in its administration that terms like "thinly-veiled metaphor" do not apply because the veil has been utterly dropped. Cameron may as well be standing nose to nose to us and screaming about the cold, ruthless, horrific brutality of game hunting; the cold, ruthless, horrific brutality of modern military "tactics"; the ugly, arrogant, mindless jingoism of Americans (depicted here through the lens of all humans, or Sky People), and of the military; the boundless spirituality and wisdom of indigenous peoples all over the world, and their mindful relationship with the natural world, accentuated in the Na'vi as they are once again one for one stand-ins for the native peoples of any continent; the importance of family; and so on. If any given viewer doesn't loathe modern civilization with all its destructive, harmful waste before sitting to watch, one certainly should after. Yes, all such sentiments are most welcome at large, but a little tact would have gone a long way in this cinematic blockbuster.And it still must be said that for as fabulous as the CGI is, 'The way of water' is nonetheless again an illustration of the limits of post-production effects. The world of Pandora and all within is marvelous beyond what words can concisely describe, but the more that CGI is required to achieve in some moments, the less sure-footed it is. Some of the flashier underwater effects, for example, namely bioluminescence, ride the line between grand and gauche. Moreover, part of the weakness of CGI like this is that when you rely on it for truly every last tidbit, it must necessarily be flawless, or the slightest inclusion that is Lesser Than will stick out - and if only for a fraction of a second, some slight inclusions stick out. Some shots of Na'vi characters are very simply weaker than others, and where these active elements are but one of many facets of a scene they may not come off so well; part of this is just owing to the lesser designs of some characters, but there's also an unfortunate truth that the very best of CGI, and motion-capture technology, just can't do everything all the time, no matter what some filmmakers or studios want us to believe. Emphasizing all the above points, both good and bad, is the action. Far, far more than not, the action sequences are brilliant. They are fast-paced but not frenetic, a fine credit to the editing team, and exquisitely orchestrated, with fluidity and violent impact that's darn near poetic in their own way; see, for example, the epic battle in the last act, and the climax among a smaller subset of characters. There are also times, though, when little odds and ends in the action are altogether over the top. And as one last criticism that must be noted, when a title such as this tries so hard to do so much, there will inevitably be some minutiae that get lost along the way, be it aspects of the story that could have been explored more, or characters and character traits that could have been capitalized upon to greater effect (e.g., Neytiri, and her startling mindset at a key juncture in the last act).Still, for all the doubts I had from well before I ever saw this, and for all the scrutiny and harsh verbiage that one may see fit to lay on the shoulders of such a colossal release, the fact remains that this 'Avatar' film is actually, genuinely, outstanding. For all the doubts I had as I began to watch, and for all the criticism I've remarked upon, overall I could hardly be happier with how good it is. The final impression I'm left with, even with caveats, is of a cinematic experience that transports us and takes us on an incredible journey. If this is not an indication of how successful 'The way of water' is, then nothing is. I'm a cynic and a skeptic, but I'm glad that in this case, I was mostly proven wrong. It won't appeal to all comers, by any means, nor meet with equal favor among all, but take it from someone whose expectations were middling and who steps away fulfilled: 'Avatar: The way of water' is well worth the proverbial price of admission, and I'm pleased to give it my high and hearty recommendation!

author: banasanasizene
text:
James Cameron's *Avatar: The Way of Water*, the long-awaited sequel, finally hit the screens after 13 years. With its visual effects, underwater sequences , the film is nothing short of enchanting. Yet, beneath all this technical brilliance lies a story devoid of emotional depth, riddled with clichés.A Visual Triumph, But...
The film undoubtedly offers one of the most stunning visual experiences in cinema history. The details in the underwater scenes, the vibrancy of the color palette, and the advancements in motion capture technology are truly commendable. However, this technical perfection isn't enough to mask the film's weak screenplay.Storyline: Predictable and Lacking Innovation...
Avatar 2 follows almost the same blueprint as its predecessor: Jake Sully and his family face a new threat, bond with a local tribe, and fight to protect nature. The villains operate with the same motivations, and character development remains minimal. The addition of child characters doesn't add emotional depth-instead, it turns the film into an extended family melodrama.
