author: coolzmadani
text: James Cameron returns to the world of Pandora over a decade after the groundbreaking success of Avatar with Avatar: The Way of Water-a sequel that expands the universe both visually and emotionally. The result is a film that's a technical marvel and a heartfelt exploration of family, identity, and survival, though not without some narrative flaws.Set more than ten years after the events of the original, The Way of Water follows Jake Sully (Sam Worthington), now fully integrated into Na'vi society, as he and Neytiri (Zoe Saldaña) raise their family in a time of uneasy peace. That peace is shattered when the Sky People-humans-return to Pandora with a new mission that threatens the Na'vi way of life. Forced to flee their forest home, Jake and his family seek refuge with the oceanic Metkayina clan, adapting to a new way of life in hopes of avoiding conflict.The most immediately striking aspect of the film is, unsurprisingly, the visuals. Cameron once again pushes the boundaries of filmmaking technology, particularly with his use of underwater performance capture. The aquatic environments are lush, vibrant, and teeming with fantastical marine life that makes Pandora's oceans as immersive and captivating as its forests were in the first film. Every frame feels carefully constructed, and the visual effects are seamlessly integrated into the storytelling.The film also delves deeper into the world-building of Pandora. The Metkayina clan and their oceanic culture provide a fresh lens through which to view this alien planet, with new customs, creatures, and spiritual beliefs. This expansion of the Na'vi mythology feels natural and adds texture to the universe.Character-wise, the sequel places a strong emphasis on family dynamics. Jake and Neytiri's children-Neteyam, Lo'ak, Kiri, and Tuk-are central to the story, and their perspectives offer a younger, more emotional angle. Lo'ak (Britain Dalton), in particular, gets a significant amount of screen time as he struggles with living in his older brother's shadow and finding his place in a world of constant upheaval. Kiri (Sigourney Weaver, impressively playing a teenager) is another standout, her mysterious origins hinting at a deeper connection to Pandora itself.While the visuals and emotional beats hit their mark, the narrative occasionally stumbles. The core conflict-humans returning to conquer Pandora-is similar to the first film, and though the family dynamic adds complexity, some storylines feel underdeveloped or familiar. The film's length (over three hours) can be felt in the slower middle section, where the focus on exploring the ocean world drags the pace despite the visual wonder.Stephen Lang returns as Colonel Quaritch, now resurrected in an avatar body. His presence adds a personal vendetta to the broader colonial narrative, though his motivations don't evolve much from the first film. The film hints at potential growth or moral conflict, but it never fully commits to exploring them in depth.The score by Simon Franglen (building on the late James Horner's themes) complements the film beautifully, blending natural sounds with sweeping orchestration. It reinforces the emotional and spiritual tone of the film, especially during the more poignant or awe-inspiring scenes.In conclusion, Avatar: The Way of Water is a stunning visual experience and a worthy successor to the original. It broadens the scope of the Pandora universe, introduces compelling new characters, and explores themes of family, identity, and environmental stewardship. Though it occasionally falters in pacing and narrative originality, the film succeeds in reigniting the magic of Avatar while charting a course for future installments. It's not just a return to Pandora-it's a deeper dive into its heart.

author: gnperuti
text: How do you follow up quite possibly the most ambitious visual effects extravaganza in film history? By not only topping the ambition, but giving us a story and characters along with it that's actually halfway decent. Surprisingly, James Cameron doesn't cram as many cliches into the script this time around. There are a few, like the stock bullies, but nowhere near the numbers the first film had. There are some neat ideas, like the villains actually learning about Na'vi culture to hunt the heroes better. I love seeing the new society introduced here and the various ways they live. And the characters, both old and new, may still not be the most interesting, but they're strong enough to hold my interest more than the first, though Zoe Saldana does ham it up a little too much towards the end. I even like the arcs given to the characters of Lo'ak and Kiri, and am interested to see where the latter goes in the sequels. Honestly, the only thing the first film has on this is it's shorter. The film really does feel as long as it is, especially if, like me, you try watching it in theaters when two hours into this three hour movie, you need to use the bathroom.The effects in the first film were a massive game changer, there's no denying it. They were amazing in 3D, still look spectacular in 2D, and have aged exceptionally well. So, when I say the effects in this film make the ones in that one look like a 70s B movie, rest assured that I'm not saying that lightly. Pandora looks as gorgeous as it ever did, both among the natives and the humans. I really enjoy looking at the many new machines and vehicles employed by the villains; the massive ship used by the hunters is especially cool. But, if the scenes above water are impressive, they're nothing compared to the ones underwater. It legitimately looks like they really filmed this under the sea; not once did it feel CG. The lighting, the muted colors, the many flora and fauna, it's absolutely breathtaking; I'd almost recommend muting the movie during these scenes to just admire the imagery. The music's still amazing, including a great theme song by The Weekend. And the action's a lot of fun too, even if the climax does come off as Cameron trying to recreate Titanic.Overall, if not for the ludicrous runtime, Avatar The Way Of Water would probably get a nine. As it is, it's still a rare sequel that's superior to the original, since I was invested in something other than the effects this time. As for the upcoming third one, I don't know if I'll see it in theaters, since it's supposedly longer than this, but I'll definitely watch it on streaming.

summary: Back to the world of pandora
text: After more than a decade of anticipation, Avatar: The Way of Water delivers a mesmerizing and immersive cinematic experience that transports audiences back to the world of Pandora. Directed by James Cameron, the sequel expands on the themes and visual grandeur of the original 2009 film while introducing new environments, cultures, and emotional stakes. It is not merely a continuation of the first movie-it is an evolution that deepens the lore of Pandora while showcasing groundbreaking technological advancements.The story follows Jake Sully and Neytiri, who have built a life together and now have a family. However, their peaceful existence is once again threatened by the return of human invaders, forcing them to leave their home and seek refuge with the Metkayina, a water-dwelling Na'vi clan. This transition from the lush forests to the vast oceans of Pandora is one of the film's most exciting aspects. It introduces viewers to an entirely new ecosystem, teeming with stunning underwater creatures and awe-inspiring seascapes. The Metkayina people, with their unique adaptations to ocean life, add a fresh perspective to the world-building, making Pandora feel even more expansive and lived-in.One of the most outstanding aspects of The Way of Water is its visual effects. James Cameron and his team have once again pushed the boundaries of CGI, motion capture, and 3D technology. The underwater sequences, in particular, are breathtaking, with an unparalleled level of realism in how characters move and interact with the aquatic environment. The creatures, the way sunlight filters through the water, and the intricate bioluminescent details make every underwater moment feel like a masterpiece. Watching this film in IMAX 3D enhances the experience, making it feel as if you are truly diving into Pandora's oceans.Beyond its visual spectacle, the film shines in its exploration of family dynamics. Jake and Neytiri's children play a crucial role in the story, and their individual journeys add emotional depth to the narrative. The sibling relationships, struggles with identity, and the pressure of living up to expectations are all explored in meaningful ways. One of the standout characters is Kiri, an adopted daughter with a mysterious connection to Pandora and Eywa, the spiritual force that binds all life on the planet. The film also introduces Spider, a human boy raised among the Na'vi, whose presence adds layers of complexity to the central conflict.The action sequences are intense and beautifully choreographed, especially in the latter half of the film. The final battle is both visually spectacular and emotionally gripping, blending stunning cinematography with high-stakes action. While the middle portion of the movie slows down to focus on the characters adapting to their new environment, the beauty of the underwater world and the emotional beats keep it engaging rather than dragging.The musical score, composed by Simon Franglen, stays true to the spirit of James Horner's original work while bringing in new elements that enhance the emotional and epic moments. The sound design is equally impressive, immersing the audience in both the serenity of the ocean and the intensity of battle.Ultimately, Avatar: The Way of Water is a cinematic event that must be experienced on the biggest screen possible. It is a visually groundbreaking film with an emotional core that makes it more than just a technical marvel. While some may find its simple plot and long runtime to be a drawback, the sheer beauty, emotional weight, and immersive storytelling make it a worthy successor to the original. This is a film that reaffirms James Cameron's ability to transport audiences to new worlds, making them feel deeply connected to the characters and the environment they inhabit. It is not just a movie-it is a breathtaking journey that leaves a lasting impression.

The Aztecs were notorious for their ritual human sacrifices, capturing enemies from other tribes to offer to their gods. Similarly, the Incas expanded their empire through subjugation and assimilation, often waging brutal campaigns to maintain control over their territory.This narrative, which paints the "evil" European and "progress" as the core problems of our world while idealizing alien civilizations that supposedly live in a sort of prehistoric state (perhaps the Stone or Bronze Age, as we might speculate from their technology and culture), is growing tired.Ironically, what makes Cameron's Avatar truly exceptional is precisely the advanced technology and science that brought its stunning visual effects to life - everything the fictional Navi civilization fundamentally opposes.

author: JaydoDre
text: One's ability to enjoy this film will be tied to one's expectations. What did you think of the first film? It was a visual spectacle, with fairly good performances and a simple, at times silly, script. And that is what this movie delivers as well - over 3 hours of excellent visual candy surrounded by Cameron's environmentalist misanthropist propaganda. The primary complaint I hear about Avatar 2 is that it has a weak underdeveloped story, but what artistic depth did you exactly expect going in?The story is simple, but its primary function is to drive us to new cool-looking environments. As the subtitle of the movie suggests, most of the story plays out in a water world (can't wait for Avatar 3: The Fire Nation), which brings with it a new canvas for visual artists to show off their creativity.While the story isn't noteworthy, there is something noteworthy about the anti-human theme. In the first film, the humans were unequivocally portrayed as the bad guys, exploiting and destroying the indigenous population, all because of some exotic mineral. In the sequel, however, the story makes it clear that humans are fighting for survival. That, coupled with a few other events, made me increasingly side with the humans, but the film still very clearly wants to tell you that the white man is evil and shows the humans being slaughtered in large numbers, even when they are just going about their business, not attacking anyone.You know, Mr. Cameron, it is a little strange to expect your audience to pay to see your movie but then also tell them how much they suck. Of course, Avatar is just a silly action-adventure cartoon, but I thought I'd point out the contradiction.A few characters who died in the first movie are brought back from the dead through awkwardly shoed in sci-fi magic. The acting in the first film was good, so it makes sense to bring those actors back, but the method of their return feels so forced.Avatar: The Way of Water is meant to be seen in 3D on a large screen, just like its predecessor. Unfortunately, this fact greatly diminishes the movie's value once that thing arrives to your TV, unless you have some massive 3D home cinema installation. If you see this movie the way it was meant to be seen and you don't go in expecting anything more than cool visuals, you won't be disappointed.

author: chiragrathod09
summary: *A Drenched Masterpiece of Emotion and Vision*
text: James Cameron does it again! "Avatar: The Way of Water" takes us on an unparalleled emotional and visual odyssey that transcends the boundaries of cinematic storytelling. Set against the breathtaking backdrop of Pandora's oceans, this film delves deeper into the Na'vi culture and their symbiotic relationship with nature, inviting viewers to experience the beauty and fragility of their world in stunning detail.The advancements in visual effects are nothing short of revolutionary. Every drop of water feels alive; the bioluminescent creatures pulse with breathtaking realism, and the expansive underwater landscapes are a testament to the artistry and engineering triumphs of the filmmaking team. It's an experience that goes beyond mere viewing-it's a dive into a vivid dreamscape that immerses you entirely.But it's not just a spectacle; the narrative weaves a tale that is both epic and intimate. We follow Jake and Neytiri, who must navigate the complexities of family, loyalty, and sacrifice against the looming threat of re-colonization. The film's emotional core is powerful, with characters that resonate deeply, reminding us of the importance of environmental stewardship and the bonds we share with each other and our world.The performances are rich and nuanced. Zoe Saldaña and Sam Worthington deliver heartfelt portrayals, adding layers to their characters that elevate the stakes of their journey. Newcomers to the cast, including Kate Winslet, bring fresh energy and depth that enhance the sprawling narrative.Cameron's direction is masterful; he balances the grandiosity of action sequences with poignant, quiet moments that allow for reflection. The film's pacing is expertly crafted, allowing the audience to soak in the beauty of Pandora before plunging them into thrilling confrontations that keep your heart racing."Avatar: The Way of Water" is not just a sequel; it's a statement-an artistic achievement that pushes the envelope of what cinema can achieve. With themes of love, loss, and the fight for what is right, it resonates on an emotional level that stays with you long after the credits roll.In a world where spectacle often overshadows substance, James Cameron reminds us that at the heart of every great story lies the human experience. This film isn't merely watched; it is felt-an unforgettable journey that beckons us back to the beautiful waters of Pandora and beyond. Don't miss your chance to experience this marvel on the big screen!

author: akitaonrails
summary: Not bad. But expected way more.
text: I had the opportunity to watch Avatar: The Way of the Water in the 4D IMAX room at TCL Chinese Theater in Los Angeles while I was there on vacation a few days ago (jan 2023). Highly recommend there; it's not a crowded room though I don't care about 4D seats. They move, have some mild air jets, and that's it. More important is the high framerate that gives the 3D effect a much sharper look. I'm not sure if my session was a fixed framerate or variable; if it was variable, I didn´t notice. I was fully immersed in the movie.Again, this Avatar's gimmick is the projection room's technology. The first Avatar debuted in 3D in theaters, and this second Avatar perfects it. That's the gist of it and why you want to watch it in a good IMAX 3D theater. CGI finally reached true photorealism, which doesn't feel like cheap videogame cut scenes. Yes, it has an artificial tint, but it's not a cheap experience. You know it was expensive.Because of audio and visual production value alone, this movie is a 10/10. But the story leaves a lot to be desired, and it is not even a 4/10. So I will average it to a fair 7/10 experience.The acting and the casting were spot-on. Every actor brought their A-game to this movie, especially if you consider that everybody had to act under very annoying motion capture suits all the time. Remarkably, they were all able to do it. Even more so, considering that they had several stunt people acting in the underwater sequences. I was very captivated by the performances. Sigourney Weaver deserves extra kudos for perfectly portraying a 14-year-old troubled teenager. I didn´t know it was her today. I really thought it was a very talented young actress playing Kiri.I don't have any complaints about the actors and stunt people. The same goes for the audio effects and soundtrack. Combined with the CGI visuals, they complemented each other to a beautiful underwater ballet. As I said, the production values alone are worth the value of admission.My only complaint is the screenwriting. It was comparably very weak, full of plot holes and easy shortcuts. The first Avatar is yet another version of the Pocahontas story. Evil greedy colonizers bully the poor native Navis and destroy the ecosystem. And again, those same evil colonizers are back. Worse, they are all portrayed as comically stupid and very unbelievable. People are not evil just for the sake of being evil or just blindly going after easy cash. Well, yeah, there are scammers like that. But 2 movies in, any futuristic government would have played the diplomacy card by now, especially now that Jake Sully and his crew are fully embedded within the Navi community. Really, a few Zoom meetings would have avoided a lot of headaches. The expensive headache, I should add. The economics of the whole invasion makes no sense whatsoever. And yes, costly endeavors do take economics into consideration.It feels cheap when every evil character is yet another Coyote after Road Runner.Even though the world-building clearly had a lot of attention, the screenwriting broke the experience again. When Jake Sully and his family had to flee to the sea community, the sea aliens were depicted as a bunch of a-holes and bullies. The entire 2nd act is the concept of forest Navis having to adapt to life underwater. And the sea people are harsh, like, "hey guys, don't bully those forest monkeys too much. Yes, they are weak and useless, and babies have better water skills, but let's be nice with them". They literally say it like that. The bullying is relentless, so you assume that, yeah, it makes sense. As a human being, I would struggle to hold my breath underwater for several minutes.So there is this sequence of montages of the Sully family struggling and learning to live there. But then we move to the evil crew looking for them, realizing that only a little time has passed. Days, maybe a few weeks. I was expecting something like "a few months later," at the very least. But then, all of a sudden, the forest family is super comfy underwater. What gives? Wasn´t it super tricky? Are all of them coincidentally gifted? That broke the story for me.The 3rd act makes no sense whatsoever. Without giving a lot of spoilers, the sea aliens are very inconsistent. They have absolutely no murder code. Not even for revenge. But then the evil people kill their relatives, and everybody is like, "they have to die today." Didn't you outcast your own because he took revenge on the murderers of his kids? All of a sudden, it's allowed?? And when we reach the final battle, it's only the Sully family against the evil guys, and everybody of the sea people disappears? It could be more consistent.The writing is very shallow, most of the characters are very shallow, and the evil colonizers are Coyote-level stupid. The acting tries its best. I'm amazed they could play convincing characters with this level of poor writing. Seriously.I also understand that they wanted to put Sully as a supporting character this time and his kids in the forefront. It does work as the kids are very well played. But the way they put Sully and Neytiri aside felt like character assassination. Compare them in both movies; it's unjustifiable. Again, the way they did it is bad writing. So the conclusion is that the Achilles' hill of this movie is the writing. Hollywood is in dire need of better screenwriters.I think Avatar is a movie worth watching in theaters because of its unique 3D experience, but no one will call it a masterpiece for its writing. There are kids' movies with a better plot.The only reason Avatar's box office surpasses Top Gun is because of that unique 3D experience. But Top Gun is a superior movie overall, no doubt about that. The incentive is that watching Avatar on a smartphone is a waste of time, it is all about blue people under blue water. It would just be a blue mess in a tiny screen. It requires IMAX.So yeah, 7 out of 10 is very generous.

author: fadybaseleem
summary: A Cinematic Tsunami of CGI, but the Plot is Just a Ripple!
text: Avatar 2 splashes onto the screen with jaw-dropping visuals and mind-blowing special effects that'll make your eyes pop like a Na'vi's. The underwater scenes are so mesmerizing, you might start checking for gills on your neck! But hey, hold up, it's not all smooth sailing in this ocean of CGI wonders.While the movie dives deep into the ocean, the story stays afloat on familiar shores. It's like déjà vu all over again as we see echoes of the first Avatar. The characters, well, some of them are as deep as a puddle, lacking that extra dimension that would make them truly dive-worthy. And let's not forget the sudden shifts in focus that can leave you feeling like you're caught in a rip current.This sequel is like a rollercoaster ride through an underwater world, with highs and lows that'll leave you gasping for air. The pacing can be as choppy as the sea on a stormy day, with some parts feeling like they're treading water for too long. At nearly 3 hours, you might find yourself wishing for a life raft to rescue you from the boredom.In the end, Avatar: The Way of Water is a cool dive into a visually stunning world, but it's not without its rough waters. It's like a treasure chest with some shiny gems but also a few sea cucumbers. With a bit of editing magic, trimming about 20 minutes could turn this voyage from a marathon into a sprint without losing any of its charm. author: Obiigs
text: « Avatar: The Way of Water" emerges as a cinematic enigma that, despite its breathtaking visuals and groundbreaking effects, falls short in narrative depth and character development. The film's ambitious attempt to transport viewers back to the lush world of Pandora is marred by a plot that seems stretched thin over its extensive runtime.The sequel's reliance on spectacle over substance leads to a storyline that feels recycled and predictable, lacking the originality that made its predecessor a standout. The characters, while visually stunning, fail to evoke the emotional connection necessary to drive the story forward, leaving the audience adrift in a sea of stunning imagery without a compelling anchor.Moreover, the dialogue often borders on the banal, with attempts at profundity coming off as trite rather than insightful. The film's antagonists, particularly the human military forces, are painted with broad strokes, their motivations unclear and their actions serving more as plot devices than as genuine threats.In essence, "Avatar: The Way of Water" is a testament to the power of visual effects but also a reminder that even the most beautiful of films can lack the soul needed to make a lasting impact. It's a reminder that cinema is not just about what we see, but also about what we feel, and in this regard, the film struggles to resonate on a deeper level.

author: 1thousand-movies
text: Overall, my impression of the movie was mixed.I was truly impressed by the stunning graphics, which brought the world of Pandora to life in vivid detail. The breathtaking scenery and mesmerizing creature designs made for some truly awe-inspiring moments, particularly in the scenes where characters rode on the back of creatures through the air or underwater. These sequences felt immersive and made me feel like I was there alongside them.However, despite the visual spectacle, I found myself frustrated by the pacing of the film. The lengthy exposition took too much time to set up the story, with over an hour devoted to establishing the characters' backgrounds and the world they inhabit. This prolonged introduction felt excessive and detracted from the overall momentum of the plot. Additionally, there were several instances of filler content, particularly in the form of predictable teenage drama, which added little to the overarching narrative.Ultimately, while I was captivated by the movie's impressive visuals, I couldn't help but feel that the story itself fell short. If not for the stunning graphics, I would have rated the film a 4.

author: lor_
text: IMDb is a clearinghouse of controversy about the 2nd Avatar movie by James Cameron -pretty much debating about what the filmmaker chose as his script's main focus and how it measures up with expectations.He has never been one of my favorite filmmakers, as I tend to favor movies about ideas rather than action/SFX. Growing up, my favorite sci-fi movies tended to be "THX 1138" (I sat through it at a Philadelphia theater 3 times in a row in first-run), "Colossus: the Forbin Project", "The Andromeda Strain", "Silent Running", etc., not blockbusters.But based on his track record of making movies that were so successful with mass audiences, Cameron is able to command resources not available to many of his peers, I suppose Christopher Nolan or Ridley Scott being in the same category. He is also able to decide the direction of his content.So in "The Way of Water" he has channeled his obvious interest in environmental causes (even such crusades as quaint but important as the "Save the Whales" movement of a generation ago) into a story whose center is focused on the adolescent characters, rather than the first film's romantic leads and militaristic/conqueror villains (though in a supporting role the versatile Edie Falco excels). Coppola did this with "The Outsiders", but of course he represents filmmakers who ultimately left the arms race of "bigger and bigger" movies (and astronomical budgets) to focus on smaller, personal projects, after the failure of his innovative studio American Zoetrope and later on the flop called "Godfather 3".So I can and do admire the craftsmanship, heart and technical innovation of this "Avatar" sequel (as well as its amazing attention to detail that big money can buy) without it being among my favorite cinematic experiences. I suspect documentaries could represent Cameron's small-scale outlet in future while completing the rest of the "Avatar" sequels, but in a world where spectacular is synonymous with success (even "Barbie" and "Oppenheimer" fit this bill), small projects don't seem to count. Hopefully this trend will reverse, perhaps if a budget retrenchment (as occurred in the late '60s) occurs, with the exorbitant spending by competing streaming services, notably Netflix, likely to implode.

author: scaryjase-06161
text: I know a lot of people loved, loved, loved Avatar, but I was very much not one of them. There was no doubt it looked impressive, but I found it an overly long version of a story that I just didn't care for - so it's safe to say I'm not exactly looking forward to this.Dear God, there's 3:12 of the thing. ONE HUNDRED AND NINETY TWO MINUTES! Who needs that?!? If I had just one guess, I suspect I'd go for "not me".Well, I did it! ALL the way through and boy was it a struggled. There's no doubt that a lot of the components of the film are impressive and I promise I'll try to remember to mention some of them. But......there's a very fine line between "epic" and "dull" and this film sees that line, speeds over it and leaves it for dust in the rear view mirror. It also desperately wants me to care about the characters - and I just don't. I don't know if it's because they're animated or because they are aliens or because they're not particularly well written - but I really don't care if all of them and their beautiful planet gets entirely destroyed. In fact, I'd destroy it myself if it meant the film finished in half the time.Actually, I'm not being entirely fair there - if it was half the time, then I might have cared an awful lot more about it all. There is a decent enough (but not great or particularly original) story hiding in there and there were some moments in the last hour where I did feel slightly engaged - but even they were spoiled because......there are too many setpieces which are only there to provide a visual spectacle but they add nothing to the plot - they would be impressive (although still too long) if part of a David Attenborough documentary, but all you've got here is the imagination and ability of the animators. There is, however, no doubt that they are very able animators (IMDB lists 63 of them!) - there's some very impressive visuals on display in pretty much every frame of the film. I found the "animated" humans particularly intriguing - they manage to somehow look real and fake at the same time.My other major talking point is that for a film with such a stellar cast, a lot of the voice acting isn't great - it's all very over the top. The baddies in particular are all very pantomime villain and some of the other characters have very poorly written motivations, so I guess the cast were just working with what they'd been given but, once again, it didn't help me care about things.Wikipedia tells me this film has grossed over $2 billion worldwide, which is an absolutely mad amount of money. And, joy of joys, that means we're going to get Avatar 3, 4 and 5!! Wikipedia also explains why it didn't appear in The Guardian's list with their critic having described it as having a "scathingly bland plot" - I agree with the sentiment, although I remain unsure about the use of the word "scathingly" there!You know what (and this might surprise you) I really didn't like this film (although I did enjoy picking that quote as the post title) and I am completely mystified by its popularity. If you want to watch it you can find it in all the usual places, but I struggle to imagine why anyone would want to do that to themselves.

author: tonosov-51238
text: Coming back 13 years later, swinging for the fences with a trilogy that is now evidently going to be five movies. Cameron delivers a very simple rethread of the first one that hopefully will result in something wonderful down the pipeline because clearly this movie serves almost no purpose but to re-introduce the characters that the next three movies are going to revolve around.These characters range from a death flag collector to Quaritch, who was foreseeably brought back to life when Cameron revealed that humans have achieved a tangible pathway to eternal life. It makes you wonder why, after achieving this monumental milestone, they have any problems with the amorphous "dying Earth" problem. Come on. You figured out consciousness copying and cloning, but you can't terraform any other planet but Pandora? Well, it's world-building stuff.Regardless, whatever Quaritch is going through is certainly the most interesting part of the movie. Neytiri gets completely shafted until the end, and Jake just spins around with his character, learning what he should have known at the end of the first one. Actually, the way this movie reestablishes Jake sometimes makes you forget he was a human at some point. He makes very stupid decisions to move the plot along, no doubt. He was always privy to what humans were planning for Pandora, so his flight from his tribe is such a poor justification because there is no way he would ever think this would keep him or his tribe safe. Nonetheless, it is worth considering that the "government's" plan for Pandora is just so nebulously evil, which makes it entirely possible that they would go to the extent of resurrecting an entire squad of Avatars for the sole purpose of collecting one scalp.On the other hand, as much as Kiri strives to be a very likeable character, I don't think Sigourney Weaver was the right choice. It is a coin flip between her sounding vaguely like a teenager and a complete raspy grandmother, and this is undoubtedly going to get worse in the subsequent movies. And by God, if these allusions to Spider being attracted to her are not just in my head, this is going to get very awkward.Oh yeah, and the visuals. Do I really need to say anything? Although one thing I must groan about is the Metkayina cultural "allusions," if Omatikaya were vaguely a melting pot of native aspects mixed together to create their own identity, then Teal Navi are so unambiguously aping Polynesians that it's downright embarrassing in some scenes.

author: PedroReviews
summary: Avatar: The Way of Water - A Return to Pandora, With Depths and Shallows
text: James Cameron's long-awaited sequel, Avatar: The Way of Water, takes us back to the vibrant moon teeming with bioluminescent flora and fauna. This time, we delve deeper, literally, into the breathtaking underwater realms as Jake Sully and Neytiri navigate new challenges alongside their growing family.Visually, the film is a feast for the senses. Cameron, a maestro of cinematic spectacle, crafts stunning underwater sequences that transport you to a world alive with vibrant colors and awe-inspiring creatures. Bioluminescent fish dance through coral reefs, colossal aquatic leviathans glide with grace, and the sheer scale of Pandora's oceans leaves you breathless. It's a testament to cutting-edge technology and Cameron's vision.However, while the visuals are undeniably impressive, the narrative treads familiar waters. The core themes of environmentalism and colonialism, while relevant, are revisited without offering much new ground. The plot, though engaging, follows a predictable trajectory, relying on familiar beats and archetypes. Character development, especially for the new generation, feels somewhat underdeveloped, leaving you wanting more emotional depth.Despite these shortcomings, The Way of Water offers a solid cinematic experience. The action sequences are thrilling, the world-building captivating, and the message of protecting our planet resonates. It's a film that entertains, visually astounds, and encourages reflection.So, is it worth diving in? If you're looking for a visually stunning spectacle that reignites your love for Pandora, then absolutely!

author: fernandoschiavi
summary: James Cameron films an extension of the family theme and also the relationship between society and nature in another unforgettable visual spectacle full of action and emotions
text: More than a decade has passed since the release of "Avatar (2009)". Directed by James Cameron ("Titanic"), the film that became the highest grossing film of all time made history and changed the way cinema was made forever. With this baggage, any franchise would have a huge responsibility when it comes to producing a sequel. Cameron's dream has always been to continue the stories of Pandora and the Na'Vi population in the best way possible. After revolutionizing the use of 3D in cinema and popularizing the use of motion capture, the Oscar-winning director saw the need to break (once again) paradigms and deliver a sequel that not only honored the legacy of the original, but also elevated the level of technical perfection. In the end, we see another spectacle that again inherits some narrative defects from the first adventure.The beginning of "Avatar: The Way of Water" is eye-catching. The look is even more polished. So much so that the level of detail in this world full of textures that seem organic is frightening. Resuming the parallel with the films from the Marvel Universe - the biggest stars in Hollywood at the moment -, there is no comparison between the images from James Cameron's new film and those that come out of the production line of the publisher that became a film studio. Back to the plot, in this initial moment evil is back, but now also in the form of avatars. The story's big aggressor is Quaritch's blue backup (Stephen Lang), the military leader who died in the first film. Escaping from Pandora's immune system, her squad representing humanity creates terror to the point that Jake's family is forced to abandon the forest in search of a safe place. The first part of the film is an introduction that reiterates the human shadow and highlights the suffering due to the imminent scenario of non-belonging. Jake deals with his children's stubbornness in a disciplinary manner, which triggers the main theme of the second part: the rise of young people to protagonism. When welcomed by the people of the waters of Pandora, the members of the stray family are crossed by complex issues that include obedience, rebellion, adequacy, love, learning and losses.In order to give younger people space in the second act of the film, James Cameron transforms Jake into a counselor who occasionally appears to decide right and wrong. In this exuberant interlude, in which Pandora's underwater fauna and flora are showcased to exhaustion, Lo'ak (Britain Dalton) becomes the most central figure. Son of Jake and Neytiri, he falls in love with the heiress of the local village, has character-forming adventures and resents the fact that he is passed over as a warrior for his older brother, Neteyam (Jamie Flatters). However, as the film is too concerned with visual sumptuousness, these affective and psychological trajectories are abbreviated to the point of becoming footnotes. Lo'ak is not defined by filial anguish nor does he have sufficient reasons to identify with a marine being considered a pariah. Using didactic devices, such as sea hunting in which each movement is explained as if we needed a manual, the experienced James Cameron weakens the emotional speech that will later be used again as firewood to burn during the climax. While visually everything seems extraordinary, the feelings at play are refined from an ordinary perspective. However, they are not very dense and deep.An interesting point about "Avatar: The Way of Water" is how it uses allusions and referential images to generate engagement. Spider (Jack Champion) is a decal of Tarzan - even called "monkey boy" -; Quaritch taking the skull from his human body directly refers to the "to be or not to be" moment in the play Hamlet, by William Shakespeare; The hunt for the sea animal, especially the obsession of the ship's captain, is a reference to Herman Melville's novel Moby Dick. However, there are three elements that do not support significant symbolism. Spider quickly loses its importance, not even justifying the blood bond with the enemy as something dramatic enough. The indirect quote from Hamlet could mean that the villainous soldier has Shakespearean contours, even more so when he discovers that the son of his human predecessor now acts on the side of the enemy. Unfortunately, it is nothing more than a moment of tribute to the bard. Just it. The sailor's fixation on the enormous prey that can give him unimaginable profitability does not have enough time to be more than a simple symptom of capitalist ambition. Therefore, James Cameron demonstrates an interesting repertoire of references, but uses them without much dramatic relevance. The feature film goes from a somewhat empty core to catharsis at the end.Even though the film returns to scenarios and situations already known to the public, the visuals dazzle thanks to the rich texture details, the lighting work and even the play with the speed of frames per second during the scenes. It is an impressive spectacle not only for the grand action scenes, but also for the more intimate moments. The film uses technical advances to bring the Na'vi closer to the public, making them palpable both through visuals and through the drama of a family fleeing the horrors of war. And if the view is already fascinating on dry land, the production doubles the bet by taking the Sully family to take shelter with the aquatic tribe. Remaking the mechanics of presenting the wonders and peculiarities of a new world, "The Way of Water" surprises once again with its imagination and execution capacity.There is a long-held concept that "water movies" are expensive and difficult to make, in part because the result is usually not convincing enough for the public. In love with the idea of aquatic filming since "The Abyss (1989)", which he built on the historic success of Titanic, and followed it during its documentary phase, James Cameron takes the challenge to heart and creates some of the richest sensory experiences in cinema in the last years. The result of years of preparation behind the scenes, the arrival at Pandora's reefs transmits all the excitement of the filmmakers to the public. To the horror of those who demand the cutting of scenes that don't advance the plot, this second part deliberately stops everything to show characters connecting with sea life. For the film, exploring the new scenario is as important as the plot itself, in the sense of existing as a work of cinema. What other form of art would be capable of generating millions of dollars in the construction of cutting-edge technological devices to record the actions of human beings amidst a ballet of alien aquatic creatures? And more: doing it in the most realistic and passionate way possible?Of course, such charm would be empty without a story behind it, and this could be the issue that will divide the "Avatar" audience once again. The plot does not escape a simplism that sometimes leaves something to be desired. Even using shameless sincerity when literally saying that it has no answers for certain situations at the moment, the text also falls into traps that make the story unnecessarily dated. It doesn't help that "The Way of Water" has trouble bringing together different plots in a fluid way. In its megalomania, the production is unable to naturally insert the reminder that evil is surrounding the protagonists. The warnings that the villains are approaching end up looking more like interruptions than an integral part of the story that the film is really interested in showing. This is a frustration that arises because, from the beginning, the film's script appears to be far superior to the original "Avatar".As an extension of the family theme comes the whole aspect of the relationship between society and nature, already part of the first film in the franchise and really the flagship of this second. Everything that happens can be interpreted from the perspective of the importance of recognizing the world around us as part of us, in addition to criticism of humanity's capitalist view of nature. But this story finally cares about the characters enough to give them personality, arcs, and charisma. It's no surprise that it's a plot that focuses so much on family and fatherhood - themes that are very important to James Cameron's previous work. Proof of this improvement is precisely when two cores that don't work very well separately come together. In addition to putting an end to the strange intercalation between these axes, this junction begins a climax so powerful that it practically erases from memory the strangeness experienced up to that point. Especially when we realize that every feature previously introduced as part of the initial exploration returns to make the action scenes even grander. In retrospect, it's curious how the big battle in "Avatar 2" echoes so many of the great moments in Cameron's filmography. It is possible to draw parallels with several classics mentioned above, as if the filmmaker drew on the screen that everything he did before was, in some way, a preparation for what he does today.The action scenes are exciting and have urgency, making you worry about the risk. And we are inserted into battles with real consequences, making the scale of the threat increasingly dangerous. However, the Colonel's return to the plot is questionable, did he really need to return? It was clear that he will be the antagonist of this franchise, the question is whether this will be able to be sustained for longer. Well here, it already seems unnecessary. And it's certainly not for lack of creativity, we could have built something from scratch, or at least ended this character once and for all. Therefore, even with some reservations, "Avatar: The Way of Water" shows that James Cameron can do it all. His strong convictions as a filmmaker, together with an excellent team that contributed greatly to this visual bang, make this one of the great films of the year.

text: Is James Cameron still the director he used to be? He loves cartoons. This is a great example of a cartoon here. It's not our favorite genre. It's not a choral film, but it's as good as one.It has to be said that this cartoon is a beautiful picture book. Free of dirt and grime, but damaged by humans. Admittedly, the whale images are sublime. Admittedly, the ecological message is sympathetic.It's sometimes difficult to recognize a character because they look so much alike, whether on land or at sea. author: danielatala8
text: There's no way around it, Avatar is a HUGE movie. The first movie, for better or worse, really changed cinema. I bought different versions on Blu-ray and watched them many times, even memorising some lines of the movie. It was truly something amazing. At least according to me, but as with all things popular it's gathered a lot of hate, memes and some infamy during the years. So it feels unreal to see the sequel appear while I myself have gone from being just a kid to becoming a full-fledged adult. And while some of the sights feel familiar and bittersweet I can say it feels great to be back in Pandora.The movie is great, it's what James Cameron is known for, perfecting sequels and making them into an experience that's bigger than its original movie, we saw that with Alien and Terminator. Here in the second movie of Avatar he does what he's always been fascinated by, water and the life surrounding it. Going to the sea was a brilliant move from the director that also feels like a natural extension of what Avatar really is. And many of its components are stunning, the design, the effects, the music are all fantastic.The actors do a great job as well, just as in the first movie.While this movie is great I think it has a few flaws and I think it's just mainly how this sequel is being written. It's a bit like how most sequels are written, bringing back the same antagonists but in another shape, kids of the protagonists etc etc. Some of it can feel a bit cliche but most of it makes sense when you watch the movie. Also with how the movie is going to end (no spoiler) I think they're gonna keep on this premise. I also think some plot points are smoothed over and there's some things that aren't really explained. Maybe it's because they want to keep viewers to see the sequel or something.As I watched the movie I was first a bit ambivalent because of my memories of how the first was and also the sound of the haters saying that I'm corny and stuff. But the movie has a charm that instantly takes over you as soon as they reach the sea, I damn near cried at some of the stuff that happens in the movie.So I guess I am corny, I like this, even if some of the plot feels familiar and even if it feels very bombastic but I still feel this movie deserves its flowers and just the amount of time it took to get here feels unreal. summary: Machine guns muscles and the same old same old
text: The main thing I kept thinking was:Why put in so much work creating the visuals and forget about the story? Why, when you could create any kind of world that is unlike our own world, decide to have lots of musclebound machine gun wielding men being macho idiots?Is that so we know they are the bad guys. Okay. I get it.If we are exploring a different culture, why did they have the same mannerisms and speech patterns as humans? Why do all the sea creatures seem so benevolent to these human like people? Do they have no enemies in the sea? Or are they so Noble and virtuous they are immune from other creatures in their environment?I think one of the reasons this movie is nowhere near as good as the first is we are getting to a point where CGI no longer amazes us like it once did. In someways the closer we get to a perfect replica, the less interesting it becomes. Think of manga animation which is simple but incredibly effective.There is something lifeless and souless about the Extreme verisimilitude of Avatar the way of the water. Thanks to motion capture the movements are so very lifelike and believable, it's almost like, meh, okay, so what? Although the way the reptile-birds fly is way too ungainly and clumsy. If these were real birds they wouldn't be able to fly at all.Also, the thoracic and cervical areas of the human like characters still doesn't look right. A bit awkward. The shoulder joint is a very complicated situation. Keep trying. Or don't.Another thing that annoyed me was the action and story mostly revolves around the male characters. Yes there are strong female characters but a lot of the movie is about the men having fights with each other or proving themselves or getting the hots for someone, the women and girls serve as accessories to a degree. I've only watched half the movie so maybe the females get more of the action later on.There is a 10 minute documentary on Disney about the making of the movie. In a Studio where you can see about 25 to 30 people working on set, only one was a woman. Maybe that has something to do with the focus of the film.The plot is very flimsy, the dialogue is awful. And it's too bloody long!I'm only halfway through. Three hours is ridiculous and unwarranted considering the lack of story. Really crazy, considering the cost and work that goes into just one second of animation. It's bizarre to think that they left so much unnecessary stuff in, amazing. I suppose being a three hour movie is supposed to make it seem more serious or something, but it really just makes it more boring than it already is.Of course the visuals are striking, the best thing about this movie are the incredible sea and land environments inspired by our incredible planet we are so Lucky to live on.

text: After booting the Earthlings off Pandora at the end of the last film, species-traitor Jake Sully, now permanently in blue-face, has settled down with his growing family of hybrids only to be called back to be the great-blue-hope and save the mawkishly spiritual natives when the incredibly awful, but usually incompetent, humans return in force. Like the first Avatar film, the CGI and practical special effects are superb but unlike the first film, we've seen it all before, so they don't make up for the simplistic story, juvenile script, and card-board acting (both by people and CGI entities). James Cameron's flair for action and techno-imagery is on display, as is his almost pathological lack of subtlety as the painfully perfect Na'vi demonstrate, like the Ewoks did before them, that technologically sophisticated weaponry is no match for spears and bows'n'arrows when the latter are wielded by the righteous and/or oppressed (wishful thinking with, sadly, little historical support). In addition to the overly-long and repetitive battle scenes, and colourful but sophomoric 'new-agey' moments, we also have to put up with a lot of 'awkward teenage blues' as the youngsters infiltrate pretty much every scene (and do exactly what you expect they are going to do). IMO, the worst decision Cameron made was to contrive to have the Na'vi be heard in English, which just highlights the weakness of the incredibly clichéd dialogue (especially that of the 'younglings', which seems to be pandering to teenage audiences as the characters all talk as though they learned the language hanging around a mall in 2020, bro). Audibly, the only thing more risible than the dialogue was the Na'vi's incessant 'hissing', a gimmicky trope that was quickly beaten to death (it didn't help that when they weren't hissing, they were speaking perfect contemporary English). All-in-all: cloying, self-righteous, excessively drawn-out, and not particularly interesting, with a premise and plot so message-driven that the entire film might as well be treated as a parable (just a different J. C.).

author: MattyLuke-81663
text: "I know one thing: wherever we go, this family... is our fortress."I remember when the first Avatar came out, it was a memorable experience to see it. It was Christmas Eve, with a rare fall of snow and rush hour traffic through the Christmas holidays in town. So, the first movie has a special place in my heart, despite its flaws. I never understood the hate the first movie received over the years. It is one thing to have an opinion, but what I find odd is every criticism people had for that film can apply to any other movie, yet Avatar somehow got it the worst. Due to it being popular, maybe?Anywhere, I was ten years when it came out, and now (as I am writing this) I am 23 years old. During that time, I finished Primary school, High school, college, and University and survived a global pandemic. So, it has been a while, and a lot has happened. This review is as late as the sequel, so it seems fitting.But how was it? I thought it was solid.Jim Cameron did it again!It is a long movie, clocking in at 3-hour-and-12-minutes, and while watching, I did feel the runtime a bit, but with a man like Jim Cameron behind the camera, he guides you through the scenes visually, with a flow in pacing, coming from a veteran of his craft.A character like Jake Sully has more to him compared to the first, with him having to raise a family and keeping his children in check. He uses his past military experience to its benefit by ordering his kids around and showing them tough love. Sam Worthington was good in this, and it helped that he has got something to work with, in terms of his character and emotional drive.Zoe Saldana is fantastic as always, even though she cries a lot in the movie.Stephen Lang is back as the villain (they explain how), and his character is a massive improvement here. Instead of being a generic evil military who is hard as nails; however, for the sequel, they take an interesting approach to the character where the actor has more to work with, like Worthington.On the other hand, the visual effects and the 3D are standouts here. Some of the best CGI ever? The water looked so realistic it puts other water effects to shame, looking at you Aquaman and The Little Mermaid remake. The world-building was compelling, and the camera work was off the charts. I don't like 3D for movies, but here it is phenomenal, especially in the underwater scenes.Although, it does take a while to get going, as I struggled to connect with it at the start. The score was not as impactful or epic since James Horner (RIP) didn't compose the score. Some of the writing was not great, especially one scene involving bullies that was so bad. Not all the emotional scenes worked for me, and it did feel manipulative.Even with those problems that I had with the movie, I understand why this movie did so well at the box office, not because of its ground-breaking story-line or characters; no, because it follows a basic theme about family, and the movie is the perfect escapism to another world that audiences have been waiting for. It's a movie that promises you an experience, a spectacle you cannot miss! It was easy enough to connect with audiences and make them revisit this world.I am more interested in Avatar 3 now than I was before.Never bet against Cameron boys.

author: Atsidewalks
summary: A Dazzling Dive into the Depths: Avatar - The Way of Water Review
text:
Avatar - The Way of Water, directed by James Cameron, is an eagerly anticipated cinematic masterpiece that takes us on a mesmerizing journey into the depths of Pandora. This long-awaited sequel to the 2009 blockbuster has raised the bar even higher, showcasing groundbreaking visual effects and an enchanting narrative that keeps you hooked from start to finish. Here's a general review with some key highlights:1. Visual Spectacle Beyond Imagination
Avatar - The Way of Water continues the legacy of its predecessor with jaw-dropping visuals that redefine what's possible in filmmaking. Cameron's commitment to pushing the boundaries of technology is evident in every frame. The underwater scenes are a sight to behold, and the bioluminescent world of Pandora is more enchanting than ever.2. A Return to Pandora
The film brings back the beloved characters of Neytiri and Jake Sully, portrayed by Zoe Saldana and Sam Worthington, respectively. Their chemistry remains as captivating as it was over a decade ago, and it's heartwarming to see them reunited.3. New Faces and Fresh Stories
Avatar - The Way of Water introduces new characters and intriguing subplots, adding depth and complexity to the world of Pandora. Notable performances from Kate Winslet and Cliff Curtis add new dimensions to the story.4. Environmental Message
As with the first film, Avatar - The Way of Water carries a strong environmental message. It explores the consequences of human exploitation and greed, underscoring the need for harmony with nature. The film's allegorical nature resonates deeply with our world's ongoing environmental challenges.5. Immersive 3D Experience
The film is tailor-made for 3D viewing. From underwater sequences to soaring flights on the back of Ikran, the 3D technology enhances the immersion, making you feel like you're a part of the action.6. A Cinematic Odyssey
With a runtime exceeding two and a half hours, Avatar - The Way of Water takes you on an epic journey through the breathtaking landscapes of Pandora. The pacing may feel a bit slow at times, but the grandeur of the world compensates for it.7. Enigmatic Soundtrack
James Horner's musical legacy is well preserved, and the soundtrack by Simon Franglen complements the film's emotional depth.In conclusion, Avatar - The Way of Water is a triumph for James Cameron and the entire team. It's a visual extravaganza that not only lives up to its predecessor but also surpasses it in terms of storytelling, world-building, and technological innovation. While it might not be a game-changer in the same way the original Avatar was, it's a worthy sequel that continues to immerse audiences in the breathtaking world of Pandora. Avatar fans and film enthusiasts alike will find this movie an unforgettable experience that's well worth the wait.

author: trinaboice
summary: The special effects are UNBELIEVABLE. Stunning! Gorgeous! Incredible!
text:
IN A NUTSHELL:
It's been 13 years since we all fell in love with the magical land of Pandora. Is the sequel worth watching? In a word, YES! In this story, Jake Sully lives with his wife and children on Pandora. Here is the description of the story from the studio: Once a familiar threat returns to finish what was previously started in the last film, Jake must work with Neytiri and the army of the Na'avi race to protect their home.THINGS I LIKED:
I had the great pleasure of attending a press screening last night. A free movie ticket is always nice, but I also got free popcorn and one of those reclining seats that lift your legs like a Lay-Z-Boy chair. So nice!All of the planned Avatar movies together are expected to cost over $1 billion. Rumor has it that they're being filmed back-to-back so that we don't have to wait as long this time! James Cameron is currently saying there will be three Avatar movies.The special effects are UNBELIEVABLE. Stunning! Gorgeous! Incredible! This absolutely must be seen on the biggest screen can you find or afford. IMAX with 3D! Everything is bigger than life, yet the smallest tear is so detailed and emotionally powerful.Critics and audiences have already been tossing around the word "experience" and I absolutely agree. This isn't just a movie but an experience. It's probably the most immersive movie I've ever seen. You FEEL like you're in Pandora. You can practically feel the water on your skin and wind in your hair. With my 3D glasses on, I honestly thought for a second that I was going to get wet during the rain scenes! When the huge creatures or watercraft fall down, you FEEL the heft of their weight and power. I remember after the first Avatar movie came out that people were watching it over and over until they became depressed that they had to live in our world and not on Pandora. Yes, that was an actual thing! A dear friend of mine became so obsessed with Avatar that he began blogging and posting so many comments on Disney's forum that the company took notice and later invited him to become a Disney Imagineer. True story!There has been a lot of talk about the frame rate that was utilized in the making of the movie. The industry standard is 24 frames per second. I got to see the movie in 3D which was really immersive and awesome. James Cameron decided that only certain scenes would use the HFR technology.Kate Winslet did all of her own underwater stunts herself. She broke Tom Cruise's record for filming underwater at 7 minutes and 14 seconds.The musical score was composed by Simon Franglen after James Horner's death in 2015.So much action.I love that the forest Na'avi look just a little bit different from the water Na'avi so you can tell who is who. Plus, it shows a type of evolution in the species that is fascinating.The imagination and creativity of the designs are ridiculously impressive. I heard someone say how amazing it was that actual humans thought of all of these creative things in the movie!I was worried about a movie that would take over 3 hours, but I admit that the time went by super fast.We all know Director James Cameron does an outstanding job creating epic moments whose scale is massive and mind-boggling, but he equally zooms into a tiny detail like a close-up of people holding hands that gives you all the feels in a grand and intimate way.Everything looks so real and seamless between the humans and the other creatures that share space on Pandora. You instantly believe it all.THINGS I DIDN'T LIKE:
I admit I was surprised that the director would basically rehash the same story from the first movie. The villain is the same. The learning curve is the same. The bullying element is the same. Some of the same characters from the first movie come back again even though they had died. What's so wrong with adding new characters to the story? I wouldn't have minded that a bit. I understand though. There were certain plot points that the director wanted to make.There isn't as much humor in the sequel as there was in the original Avatar movie.NO SPOILERS: Some characters were indistinguishable from others.That sweeping musical score from the first Avatar just didn't come back in full force like it did in the first movie.There is a birth that simply has no explanation. Will it be explained in the next sequel?We don't quite understand why the humans make the choices they do. You're embarrassed to be a human by the end of the movie, just like in the first movie. I assume we're going to get more information in future sequels.As beautiful as the movie is, I thought the poster didn't capture its essence at all.TIPS FOR PARENTS:
Partial nudity
Strong violence with various weapons (some with blood)
Profanity, including 1 F-bomb
Intense action
People and creatures die
Men hunt and kill creatures
Destruction
We see a bloodied arm rip in half.!

author: TxMike
text: Entertaining, but a bit of a let-down. As we saw in fantasy movies such as 'Back to the Future' and 'The Matrix', so much novelty is spent in the first movie that invariably the second seems a bit dull in comparison. This latest 'Avatar' movie conforms to that template.The 2009 'Avatar' was set in 2154, so this one must be about 2165 or 2170, judging by the age of Jake Sully's kids. He has managed to make his life in this world far away now that the invaders are gone. But they return! They managed to re-make themselves with Pandorian DNA so they are blue and large and can breathe the Pandorian air.And that is what this movie is about, Jake and his family have to travel to a new place, to blend in with the water people, but are being relentlessly hunted down. Now one would think, 150 or so years in the future, they would have something better than guns, guns, and more guns. But no, most of the action involves relentless gun battles. Which for me takes away a lot of the potential enjoyment.The movie is long, at over 3 hours, and part of the reason are long scenes showcasing the beauty of the created worlds and the interesting land, air, and aquatic creatures. So, while the movie is a bit short on interesting story, it is long on fascinating beauty and absolutely astounding animation.My wife and I watched it at home on DVD from our public library. A new feature I had never encountered before, you can select an audio that is more family-friendly, it cuts out the harsher dialog. In fact this should become standard, so many movies nowadays have such profanity in them, it would always be nice to select a more pleasant sound track.

author: Morey23
summary: James Cameron falls short the second time around
text: James Cameron is back at the box office with his latest blue man blockbuster. Only this time, it didn't bust the block quite like it did back in '09. I'm not sure if it was because the novelty of it all was lost on the audience the second time around, but it seemed as though the wonders of the foreign moon Pandora were a little less breathtaking than they were the first time. Seeing the movie pan out, things just felt like a sequel was made for the sole purpose of making a sequel. Some of the dialogue was cringe-worthy and hard to listen to. The story, despite its potential, felt repetitive and predictable too often (it's almost as if it didn't need to be 3+ hours long). All this culminated in a lack of emotional attachment to characters who had plenty of screen time for the audience to get acclimated to them. There were heartfelt moments shared between family, and new and exotic creatures that the N'avi people rode into battle, but it paled in comparison to the original Avatar throughout. Even Jake Sully's epic monologues fell short of what they originally had been. Initially filling transitions with emotion and tension, Sully's speeches in Avatar: The way of Water only seemed to put the ribbon and bow on the exact gift it was- a flex of the prowess of computer generated image technology that was state of the art... 13 years ago.

author: cineastFGD
summary: Never has a movie made me more sad
text: I've never seen a movie that has saddened me more. Despite the incredible beauty of the scenes, I was in tears nearly through the entire film. I loved all Avatar movies, but this one stands out, as Cameron has dropped all subtlety and is now holding the mirror to our faces. Pandora of course is Earth, the beauty of Pandora is the beauty of Earth in hyperbole, but still clearly recognizable. Unfortunately for Earth, most people on this planet behave like the sky people. So if you are rooting for the Na'ir, realize that in Cameron's view, you most likely are one of the bad guys. He picks up so many current issues, the dying of the coral reefs, the burning and destruction of our forests, the bestiality of whale hunting, the hunting and killing of elephants, rhinos, sharks and many other species for a single body part that is supposed to give us youth or virility. I'm sure I haven't captured all of them. The sentence 'Water has no beginning and no end.' is a very clear reference to the fact that pollution of our planet will inevitably affect us too.Reading the comments and complaints about a 'weak plot' or 'boring movie' makes me absolutely despair. How more obvious does he need to get before shallow viewers finally get the message? Our planet is burning, we destroy the very ecosystems that keep us alive, yet all people seem to care about is their personal entertainment.

author: Ratisbonanza

author: Christopher_Reid
text: Cameron's made some great films - Aliens is one of my personal favourites, T2 is arguably the best action movie of all time, True Lies is good, Titanic is decent if a bit bloated. But Avatar had major flaws. Practically everyone agrees - the visuals were very impressive, the world was detailed and interesting, but the actual plot and characters weren't that likeable. The message (nature good, humans and capitalism bad) is preachy and stupid.Cameron, being the genius that he is, decided to use the same characters in his sequel, with the same dull qualities and the same reliance on amazing graphics (I admit, they look amazing, a good way to show off fancy 8k OLED screens) without a good story, themes or plot to make use of them. I mean, I don't think it's a spoiler to say he brought back the same bad guy from the first movie. The bad guy we all thought was too 1-dimensional. Well, I guess he's 1.5 dimensional now. A fractal, if you're mathematically oriented. Not really an improvement.In fact, it's almost worse as now he's mostly evil... but also a bit inconsistent. Sometimes arbitrarily nice or overly trusting. We need a deeper motivation for him, some kind of vision that he thinks is good - he has to see himself as the hero.Avatar 2's problem is that I just don't care. I want to but can't. Zoe Saldana's character does absolutely nothing but scream, cry, scream, glare, shoot arrows (okay, that's kinda cool), cry, growl and scream. It's lame. I can't remember the main character's name. Or any of the others. I don't get why they do what they do. I don't feel connected to their world or stakes.Look, we have words like barbaric, tribal, backwards and uncivilised for a reason. All humans started like that - primitive and animalistic. But there's a reason we started using words rather than grunting, wearing clothes rather than leaves, using guns instead of spears, etc. We became civilised. That's not just a fashion choice, it's a critical part of progressing.It makes no sense for the Avatar people (Na'vi, whatever it is) to still be like cavemen but super advanced. It doesn't work like that. The same with Wakanda. Advanced technology isn't something you just do 'cause you feel like it. It takes decades, centuries of infrastructure, education, clothes for crying out loud, and other basic civilised things.Anyway, because of that, I find the blue (and teal) people really uninteresting and self-contradicting. They couldn't possibly have weapons that advanced but still be like tribal people who live in nature. They argue and assume things, their strategy is often terrible. I don't like them. A few are okay, ironically the ones who are more "human", who think and have motivations.The baddies are still completely superficial. They just blow up, burn and destroy stuff. That makes no sense. We cut down trees to use the wood to make buildings, houses, furniture, books, etc. Is that so bad? No, it's justified. Some animals get displaced, but that's a necessity. What matters more - 50 orangutans or 1,000 humans? But in Avatar 2, what is their motivation for the destruction?Why is there no mutually beneficial exchange going on? This part of history gets ignored. The more advanced civilisation can offer better medicine, transport, communication, clothes (pretty important), etc. The local primitive people will definitely want those things! In exchange, they can offer insights into the land, the animals and plants, etc. They can cede land to the more advanced culture in exchange for a share of the more advanced technology!One thing the baddies do is kill giant whale lobsters for their glowing yellow brain fluid. Oooh, so evil. What does the yellow goo do? Apparently it lengthens human life. Oh my, these baddies are so deeply ev- wait... extend human life? So, like, by how much?They say the goo from a lobster-whale brain is worth $80 million (in 2050 (or whatever year) US dollars I assume). But how powerful is it? Can it lengthen ten people's lives by 5 years each? A hundred people's lives by 10 years each? One person's life by 6 months? Why is this never explained?I'm sorry, but if the brain goo of a lobster on steroids can extend a lot of people's lives by a large amount, then it may well be financially worth it and morally justified to hunt the huge lobsters.Also, they don't use the rest of the carcass. One of the goodies is upset by this. What, would you prefer they cut up the carcass and sold it for other uses? Speaking of which, why don't the baddies use the rest of the carcass? Really? None of the rest of it has any value? Basic economics and the concept of incentives have gone right out the window.The acting is decent, the innovation in motion capture and CGI is good, the music is forgettable but I guess it's at least there, the story and heroes and villains have no depth or logic to their positions, the characters are boring and unlikeable. It's a little too long and convoluted, but it generally held my mild interest.There were some more touching moments near the end, but even they get ruined by histrionic wailing by you-know-who. The plot is so dumb that even a girl observes that "I'm being tied up again?!", to paraphrase. If the characters are noticing bad writing, what does that tell you?We get a major battle perhaps inspired by They Live!, but it all feels pointless because of what happens next. I really wanted a sequel (another intense personal fight) as that would have been absolutely hilarious. It's a bad sign when I want the movie to turn into a terrible parody of itself just so it becomes more enjoyable.Avatar 2 wasn't all bad, but it's not really a success either. It's terrible in terms of narrative, character motivations, logic, likeable characters, deeper themes. All it has going for it are the effects, the overall look and some action sequences and dramatic scenes here and there. I can't call it a disappointment since my expectations were already at sea level.

author: nihamromy
text: Avatar: The Way of Water is a visually stunning and captivating cinematic masterpiece that takes the audience on a mesmerizing journey into the depths of Pandora, a magical and immersive alien world. Directed by the visionary James Cameron, this highly anticipated sequel to the groundbreaking film Avatar continues to push the boundaries of visual effects, storytelling, and filmmaking.The story of Avatar: The Way of Water picks up where the first film left off, transporting us back to the lush and vibrant planet of Pandora. The narrative explores the deep connection between humans and the indigenous Na'vi people as they face new challenges and confront the forces threatening their way of life. It delves into themes of environmentalism, cultural clashes, and the power of unity, weaving a rich tapestry of emotion and meaning throughout.One of the film's greatest strengths lies in its ability to immerse the audience in a completely believable and awe-inspiring world. The attention to detail in every frame is truly remarkable, from the breathtaking landscapes to the intricately designed flora and fauna. The vibrant color palette and lush visuals create an otherworldly experience that is truly mesmerizing.The cinematography in Avatar: The Way of Water is nothing short of breathtaking. The camera work effortlessly captures the grandeur and scale of Pandora, showcasing its vast landscapes and majestic creatures in exquisite detail. The cinematographer's skillful use of light and shadow further enhances the film's visual impact, creating a sense of depth and immersion that draws the audience into the story.In terms of visual effects, Avatar: The Way of Water sets a new standard for excellence. The seamless integration of CGI with live-action footage is flawless, making it nearly impossible to distinguish between what is real and what is computer-generated. From the awe-inspiring bioluminescent creatures to the exhilarating action sequences, every visual element is executed with precision and artistry.The performances in Avatar: The Way of Water are equally impressive. The cast delivers compelling and nuanced portrayals, breathing life into their respective characters. Returning actors, such as Sam Worthington and Zoe Saldana, reprise their roles with depth and conviction, while new additions to the ensemble, including talented actors like Kate Winslet and Oona Chaplin, bring fresh energy to the story.The film's score, composed by James Horner, is a powerful accompaniment to the visuals on screen. It evokes a range of emotions, from wonder and awe to tension and excitement, enhancing the overall cinematic experience. The sound design is also exceptional, immersing the audience in the rich and vibrant world of Pandora.Overall, Avatar: The Way of Water is an extraordinary cinematic achievement that exceeds all expectations. James Cameron's visionary direction, combined with groundbreaking visual effects, stunning cinematography, an engrossing story, and memorable performances, make it a must-see film for any movie lover. It is a testament to the power of cinema to transport us to new worlds and inspire us with its beauty and imagination.Prepare to be swept away on a remarkable adventure as you witness the magic and wonder of Avatar: The Way of Water unfold before your eyes.

author: crimeagainstcreation
text: Oh yes, the CGI and particularly the under water scenes are delightful to watch, but with 13 years since the original super success, it's just not that impressive anymore, like so much of modern cinematic visual effects.
